a222.speaker: Narendra Modi, Prime Minister of India
a222.speech: It was at the 10th annual summit of the BRICS in 2018 in Johannesburg, South Africa, that Prime Minister Modi proposed for the first time his vision of "reformed multilateralism" to give major emerging powers a voice in global governance.

a222.speaker: India (at the UN Security Council)
a222.speech: India underscored that the draft resolution "seeks to hand over that responsibility to a body which neither works through consensus nor is reflective of the interests of the developing countries."

a222.speaker: Narendra Modi, Prime Minister of India
a222.speech: When India took over G20 Presidency (2022-23), Prime Minister Modi convened the Voice of Global South Summit where 125 developing countries participated.

a295.speaker: Pedro Sanchez, Spanish Prime Minister
a295.speech: Urged Benjamin Netanyahu's government not to threaten the flotilla, saying the activists aboard the vessels "do not represent a danger or a threat to Israel and therefore I hope that Israel, in this case the government of [Benjamin] Netanyahu, likewise does not represent any threat to this flotilla" ; added that he had already warned the Israeli government that the Spaniards taking part in the flotilla will enjoy "full diplomatic protection."

a295.speaker: Foreign Ministers of the Italian Republic and the Hellenic Republic (joint declaration)
a295.speech: Appealed to the Israeli government to guarantee the "safety of the participants" and asked the authorities in Tel Aviv to allow "the implementation of all consular protection measures" for their citizens ; "We, the foreign ministers of the Italian Republic and the Hellenic Republic, appeal to the women and men of the flotilla to accept the offer of the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem to safely deliver the humanitarian aid intended for the children, women and men of Gaza", halting the ongoing voyage ; "At this delicate moment, everyone must refrain from initiatives that could be exploited by those who still reject peace", without naming any specific actor.

a295.speaker: Israeli government
a295.speech: "Without calling into question respect for individual autonomy, we make this fresh appeal and recall that there is genuine willingness to get the humanitarian aid they are carrying to Gaza via Cyprus."

a295.speaker: Flotilla organisers / organisation
a295.speech: Accused "Israeli military ships" of alleged "intimidation tactics" and of having sent military ships overnight to carry out "intimidation manoeuvres", announcing that the flotilla will continue its voyage to Gaza ; said that at 05:30 GMT the flotilla was 120 nautical miles from the Palestinian territory ; said on Tuesday that one of the Italian ships had made a final request for them to stop sailing, which the activists rejected.

a295.speaker: Israeli Navy
a295.speech: Said it is ready to intercept the nearly 50 vessels bound for Gaza if they enter the risk zone.

a295.speaker: Giorgia Meloni, Italian Prime Minister
a295.speech: Criticised the activists' decision, saying this was a moment when everyone must "exercise responsibility, waiting while the peace negotiations take place."

a380.speaker: Kwesi Pratt Jnr, Managing Editor of The Insight newspaper of Ghana
a380.speech: Has criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky for publishing details of a private conversation with his Ghanaian counterpart, John Dramani Mahama, saying the action of Zelensky is unbecoming of the diplomatic responsibility he holds; accused President Zelensky of stirring controversy that could damage Ghana's relationship with different nations and international partners, including the Alliance of Sahel States.

a380.speaker: Volodymyr Zelensky, President of Ukraine (post on X)
a380.speech: “Ghana is also interested in our technologies, the production of various types of drones, and the experience Ukraine has gained during this war. Ghana is ready to finance our production, and we are ready to help our partners secure their borders”.

a380.speaker: Kwesi Pratt Jnr, Managing Editor of The Insight newspaper of Ghana
a380.speech: Questioned how Ghana would want to fall on Ukraine to secure its borders when "evidence abounds that Ukrainian intelligence officers and soldiers are assisting terrorist groups in the Sahel States to wreak havoc on citizens and communities in Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger"; asked "Secure the borders from whom?"; said Ghana's worries about border security "do not spring from threats from governments of neighbouring countries, but from the terrorists Ukraine is assisting in the Alliance of Sahel States".

a380.speaker: Kwesi Pratt Jnr, Managing Editor of The Insight newspaper of Ghana (post on X)
a380.speech: “The unelected President of Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelensky is a very desperate man and in his desperation, he is deliberately attempting to export his troubles. Unfortunately for Ghanaians, Zelensky has chosen Ghana as one of his export destinations to sow seeds…”

a380.speaker: The Insight article (by Kwesi Pratt Jnr), posted on X
a380.speech: Questioned how Ukraine could suggest that Ghana would abandon pressing domestic burdens and commit resources to finance logistics development meant to be deployed for Ukraine's three-year-old conflict with Russia. "Over the last three years, Ukraine has received approximately US$280 billion in military, financial, and humanitarian assistance with the US alone providing US$199.6 billion in military aid, US$48.8 billion in financial assistance, and US$3.6 billion in humanitarian aid," the article said; weighed this against Ghana's economic revival efforts where "Ghana is unable to pay its power sector debt of US$3.7 billion".

a380.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a380.speech: Announced "the cancellation of petrol allowance and allocation to all political appointees as part of the austerity measures his government is introducing".

a380.speaker: Kwesi Pratt Jnr, Managing Editor of The Insight newspaper of Ghana
a380.speech: Said President Zelensky, whose tenure in office has long expired and has used the war with Russia to perpetuate his stay at post, was showing signs of a "desperate man" who is "deliberately attempting to export his troubles". "Zelensky must be stopped from exporting the chaos in #Ukraine to #Ghana. His support for the terrorists in the Alliance of Sahel States has caused enough problems for us already."

a515.speaker: Mawuli Agbenu, Greater Accra Regional Director of NCCE
a515.speech: Addressing the participants, stressed that all kinds of elections in Ghana were the civic responsibility of Ghanaians who qualified to vote and, therefore, voters were not to sell their votes, neither were politicians supposed to buy the votes as was being alleged: "Politicians giving money to the electorate for votes and the electorate demanding money for their votes is not the way to go. Democracy and voting should be a civic duty and responsibility and not vote selling and vote buying as we are hearing is going on." ; "We as a National Commission for Civic Education, it is our civic duty to educate the general public, and for that matter the electorate and the youth as you are seated here now, to discourage you from such unhealthy practices of vote selling."

a515.speaker: Mawuli Agbenu, Greater Accra Regional Director of NCCE
a515.speech: Said even though the nation had had eight successful elections in the country in the past, it was not guaranteed that the December 7 election would be successful.

a515.speaker: Mawuli Agbenu, Greater Accra Regional Director of NCCE
a515.speech: Said in Ghana the youth formed the largest demographic group, "and this year we have a huge number of such groups and this particular programme for this year's election is geared towards the youth to ensure that the commission sensitises the youth to money in politics (monetisation) and misinformation, disinformation, hate speech and all others and to ensure the youth do not make themselves available for electoral violence".

a515.speaker: Salvata Mawulorm Koku, Ashaiman Municipal Director of NCCE
a515.speech: Said the youth were the future leaders and politicians used them to foment trouble and, therefore, the Commission would continue to ensure the youth know their civic responsibility ; she said Ashaiman was noted for violence but the commission would this time around ensure the youth stayed clear from violence so the existing peace they were enjoying could continue.

a515.speaker: Bright Agbagba, Senior Project Officer of IFES
a515.speech: Urged the youth to ensure they participated in the electoral system responsibly and demanded accountability from politicians and other stakeholders, adding, "tolerate each other in spite of religious and ethnic differences".

a588.speaker: US mission in Nigeria (statement, cited by Africa News)
a588.speech: Said in a statement that the fund will provide food assistance and nutritional support for internally displaced people in conflict-affected areas ; said the donation will provide food and nutritional assistance to 764,205 beneficiaries in the north-east and north-west of Africa's most populous country ; according to the US statement, the aid includes nutritional supplements for 41,569 pregnant and breastfeeding women and girls and 43,235 children through electronic food vouchers.

a588.speaker: Margot Velden, World Food Programme Regional Director for West Africa
a588.speech: Said that insecurity and funding cuts have placed northern Nigeria in the grip of an unprecedented hunger crisis ; according to Velden, the crisis could leave more than 1.3 million people without food and force the closure of 150 nutrition clinics in Borno state.

a741.speaker: Oluremi Tinubu, Nigeria's First Lady and Senator
a741.speech: Sounded the alarm over Nigeria's Tuberculosis (TB) crisis, revealing that one person dies of TB every seven minutes, despite the disease being preventable and curable; speaking at World TB Day 2025 Community Outreach in Sauka village on Monday in Abuja, described the situation as a national emergency that requires swift and decisive action to save lives: "In the short time we have spent at this event, many more lives will be lost if we do not act swiftly and decisively," citing alarming statistics from the World Health Organization (WHO) ; lamented that many Nigerians still suffer in silence due to stigma, lack of awareness, and delays in seeking medical care: "It is unacceptable that so many of our brothers and sisters continue to die from a disease that is both preventable and curable." ; "Every life matters. We must act now to stop this silent killer."

a741.speaker: Oluremi Tinubu, Nigeria's First Lady and Senator
a741.speech: Commended Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Muhammad Ali Pate, for his commitment to TB eradication through improved diagnosis, treatment, and prevention programs; emphasised that government alone cannot win the fight against TB, calling on traditional rulers, religious leaders, youth groups, the private sector, and international partners to support awareness campaigns and encourage early detection; announced a ₦1 billion pledge through her Renewed Hope Initiative to strengthen TB control efforts and improve healthcare facilities in underserved communities; confirmed that the Minister of State for Health has approved the establishment of a primary healthcare center in the community; vowed to advocate for increased funding, mobilize resources, and fight against stigma to ensure that women, children, and marginalized groups have equal access to TB care.

a741.speaker: Oluremi Tinubu, Nigeria's First Lady and Senator
a741.speech: Encouraging citizens to take responsibility for their health, stressed the importance of early detection and treatment: "If you have a persistent cough for more than two weeks, do not ignore it. Seek medical help immediately."

a741.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO) statistics (cited)
a741.speech: Cited as the source of alarming statistics on Nigeria's TB burden; Nigeria remains one of the eight countries with the highest burden of tuberculosis worldwide.

a741.speaker: Iziaq Salako, Nigeria's Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
a741.speech: Hinted that the Federal Government has intensified efforts to eliminate tuberculosis by 2030, with the upgrade of over 10,000 Primary Healthcare Centres (PHCs) and the training of 120,000 health workers; reaffirmed President Bola Ahmed Tinubu's commitment to ensuring that Nigeria is not left behind in the global fight against TB; noted that the government is expanding TB screening, diagnosis, and treatment services across public and private healthcare facilities in line with the universal health coverage agenda, and is strengthening community engagement and providing enhanced social protection for TB patients and their families; commended frontline health workers for their dedication despite the country's economic challenges, urging Nigerians to recognize their crucial role; praised First Lady Senator Oluremi Tinubu for her financial and advocacy support ; "TB is not a death sentence; it is preventable and treatable."

a741.speaker: Amobi Godwin Ogah, Chairman of the House Committee on HIV/AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria (speaking through Hon. Dominic Okafo)
a741.speech: Called for increased domestic funding to combat tuberculosis in Nigeria, warning that foreign funding is declining; emphasised that resource mobilization is crucial for Nigeria's TB response; revealed that the House of Representatives has urged the private sector to set up a TB fund, similar to what has been done for HIV and malaria, to ensure sustainable financing; commended President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for the unprecedented ₦700 billion investment in Nigeria's healthcare system, stating that the move signals the country's ability to tackle health challenges without relying heavily on foreign aid.

a741.speaker: Amobi Godwin Ogah, Chairman of the House Committee on HIV/AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria (speaking through Hon. Dominic Okafo)
a741.speech: Condemned the stigma and discrimination against people affected by TB, announcing that the House Committee will soon pass a law prohibiting such discrimination; stressed the need for increased TB screening initiatives, improved healthcare worker education, and better public awareness campaigns ; "For us to eliminate TB by 2030, we must commit, invest, and deliver."

a741.speaker: Austin Arinze Obiefuna, Board Vice Chair, Global Stop TB Partnership, Geneva
a741.speech: Said Nigeria is setting the pace in the global fight against tuberculosis through strong commitments, strategic investments, and effective delivery of TB interventions; commended Nigeria's remarkable progress in strengthening its health workforce and tackling TB, stating that the country's efforts are not only leading in Africa but also gaining recognition at the global level: "When I stand in the corridors of the WHO, the UN, or the African Union, I am proud of Nigeria's performance." ; praised the First Lady, Sen. Oluremi Tinubu, for her unwavering support and advocacy, urging the government and stakeholders to sustain the momentum ; "Nigeria is walking the talk, and this is the best way to fight TB by working directly with communities and delivering real impact."

a741.speaker: Walter Kazadi Mulombo, World Health Organization (WHO) Representative to Nigeria
a741.speech: In his goodwill message, raised concerns over drastic cuts in global health funding, warning that the progress made in the fight against tuberculosis could be reversed if urgent investments are not made; noted that global TB efforts have saved an estimated 79 million lives since 2000, but funding shortages now pose a serious threat to sustaining these gains; cautioned that disruptions in TB response, including research into advanced diagnostics, treatment, and vaccines, are at risk due to financial constraints.

a741.speaker: Walter Kazadi Mulombo, World Health Organization (WHO) Representative to Nigeria
a741.speech: Applauded Nigeria's leadership in tackling TB, highlighting the donation of TB diagnostic machines and ₦1 billion by First Lady Sen. Oluremi Tinubu through the Renewed Hope Initiative; commended the allocation of an additional ₦700 billion by the Federal Government to combat HIV, TB, malaria, and immunization, as well as the launch of a $50 million private sector strategy to accelerate TB elimination: "Nigeria is not just watching; Nigeria is taking action," urging donors, private sector players, academia, the press, and communities to join forces; reaffirmed WHO's commitment to supporting Nigeria's efforts to end TB by 2030 and called for collective action.

a741.speaker: Usman Nga Kupi, HRH the Sapeyi of Garki
a741.speech: Called for the establishment of a health center in Sauka, a densely populated community in the Federal Capital Territory, to serve as a TB diagnosis and treatment hub; emphasised that while awareness programs are crucial in tackling TB, tangible investments in healthcare infrastructure are essential for effective prevention, diagnosis, and treatment: "Sauka remains one of the large communities in the FCT without a health facility. A dedicated TB center here would not only help combat the disease but also improve overall healthcare delivery." ; commended First Lady Sen. Oluremi Tinubu and donor agencies for their commitment to the fight against TB, urging the government to translate commitments into lasting healthcare solutions.

a741.speaker: Daju Kachollom, Permanent Secretary of the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare (represented by Mr Akpan)
a741.speech: Emphasised the need for early detection, urging community members to take advantage of available screening services: "If you or anyone you know has been coughing for two weeks or more, experiencing weight loss, fever, or night sweats, please step forward for screening." ; commended First Lady Sen. Oluremi Tinubu for her unwavering support in tackling TB and acknowledged global partners such as WHO, the Global Fund, and the Stop TB Partnership for their role in strengthening Nigeria's TB response; called on traditional rulers, community leaders, and citizens to move beyond awareness and take decisive action: "Yes, we can end TB."

a741.speaker: Queen Ogbuji-Ladipo, Acting Board Chair of Stop TB Partnership Nigeria
a741.speech: In her welcome address, said that with 499,000 tuberculosis cases recorded in 2023 and one person dying every seven minutes, Nigeria remains the highest TB-burdened country in Africa and the sixth globally; emphasised the urgent need for increased investment in TB prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, especially in remote communities with limited access to healthcare; commended First Lady Sen. Oluremi Tinubu for her role in mobilizing support, noting that her donation of TB diagnostic machines has improved testing services, including at the event's community outreach in Sauka, Abuja; highlighted the launch of a $50 million private sector initiative to combat TB, urging stakeholders to sustain advocacy efforts and resource mobilization: "Together, we can end TB. Yes, we fit do am."

a1014.speaker: National Good Governance Advocates (NGGA) (report/press conference in Abuja)
a1014.speech: Stated on Thursday that the Rivers State Sole Administrator, Vice Admiral Ibok-Ete Ibas (retd.), has been commended on the provision of critical infrastructures and civil service reforms in the state, and also lauded his transformative leadership and meticulous stewardship of resources, which have driven unprecedented development in the state; in its detailed report made public at a press conference in Abuja, the NGGA celebrated Ibas for rescuing Rivers from the brink of collapse and restoring stability, security, and public confidence.

a1014.speaker: Dr. Abiodun Israel, NGGA National President
a1014.speech: In his address, recounted how Governor Siminalayi Fubara's administration plunged the state into chaos through "brazen abuse of constitutional norms," including his unlawful attempt to declare the seats of 27 elected lawmakers vacant over political differences.

a1014.speaker: National Good Governance Advocates (NGGA) (report)
a1014.speech: "The collapse of democratic institutions had become glaring... laying bare the capriciousness with which the instruments of power had been wielded. This was compounded by resurgent militancy and pipeline explosions that threatened Nigeria's oil-driven economy, creating a dagger aimed at the economic heart of Nigeria."

a1014.speaker: National Good Governance Advocates (NGGA) (report)
a1014.speech: Said Rivers has undergone a remarkable transformation under Ibas's leadership: "the pervasive climate of fear that once haunted the streets of Port Harcourt, the markets of Bori, the creeks of Bonny, and the oilfields of Ogoni has been replaced by a resurgent atmosphere of peace and assurance. Within a week of his administration, militancy was subdued, pipeline explosions ceased, and oil production stabilized, averting a national economic crisis." ; "in less than two weeks into his administration, markets had begun to hum with activity; businesses awakened from forced dormancy; and residents walked streets with that long-absent sense of safety."

a1014.speaker: National Good Governance Advocates (NGGA) (report)
a1014.speech: Commended Ibas's commitment to democratic restoration, noting his release of funds to the Rivers State Independent Electoral Commission for the August 30, 2025, local government elections: "His infrastructural projects include the reconstruction of the Rivers State House of Assembly complex and the completion of the Mother and Child Hospital, integrated into the Rivers State University Teaching Hospital network" ; On his oversight of the 150 billion naira Port Harcourt Ring Road dualization project: "his insistence on transparency and delivery has set a new standard for accountability in Rivers State governance, and we see this as an exemplar of stewardship, not self-interest."

a1014.speaker: National Good Governance Advocates (NGGA) (report)
a1014.speech: Fiercely rebutted allegations of contract inflation and treasury looting against Ibas, calling them "fabricated fiction" orchestrated by Fubara and his allies: "the allegations... accusing Admiral Ibas of orchestrating a fraudulent inflation of contracts amounting to nearly half a trillion naira... are nothing short of manufactured stories from the laboratory of political propaganda." ; It accused Fubara of sponsoring a "shameful publication, devoid of substantiation" to discredit Ibas and destabilise Rivers ahead of his potential return, warning that "his penchant for propaganda will once again plunge Rivers into political unrest if this goes unchecked."

a1014.speaker: National Good Governance Advocates (NGGA) (report)
a1014.speech: Urged continued reforms, including the completion of the State House of Assembly reconstruction and the strengthening of security through community policing: "Admiral Ibas has laid the foundation; it is the duty of all stakeholders to safeguard and build upon it." ; It called on President Tinubu to closely monitor Fubara's conduct and urged contractors like Julius Berger, MCC, and Craneburg to publicly refute the false claims ; It thanked President Tinubu for his timely intervention and praised Ibas's disciplined leadership, stating, "let Admiral Ibas not merely be remembered for stabilising a state under emergency, but for designing the foundational stones for its peaceful democratic rebirth."

a1035.speaker: Wondimu Filate, Public Relations head of the Ministry of Trade (MoT)
a1035.speech: said contraband trading of major commodities like gold, coffee and livestock continues to be a major factor in the low export performance, pointing to the lack of coordination between federal and regional governments to cut contraband trading, particularly for livestock, as a major hindrance to solving the problem ; “Lack of cooperation of stakeholders has affected the hard currency earnings from gold.”

a1035.speaker: Wondimu Filate, Public Relations head of the Ministry of Trade (MoT)
a1035.speech: claimed that the gold sector still suffers from illegal actors and that stakeholders have to work strongly to combat the problem.

a1035.speaker: Wondimu Filate, Public Relations head of the Ministry of Trade (MoT)
a1035.speech: added that the instability in the eastern part of the country has negatively contributed to hard currency earnings: “The eastern part of the country, which is the major export outlet, has been affected greatly by the instability which has harmed export earnings.”

a1035.speaker: Wondimu Filate, Public Relations head of the Ministry of Trade (MoT)
a1035.speech: explained that Khat, one of the country's major hard currency sources, has been suspended from export for several weeks in Somaliland and a few days in Djibouti, which has decreased Khat earnings.

a1035.speaker: Ministry of Trade (MoT) report
a1035.speech: indicated that the country's hard currency earnings from mining declined to USD 58 million from USD 107 million a year ago, and that khat export for the first six months of 2016/17 was over 25,644 tons with a revenue of USD 143 million, but during the first six months of the current budget year it went down to 22,386 tons.

a1088.speaker: Dk Frederick Ndossi, Director of Treatment and Care Services at Tanzania Health Promotion Support (THPS) through the 'Afya Hatua' project, on behalf of THPS Executive Director Dr Redempta Mbatia
a1088.speech: Released statistics showing HIV infections in Kigoma region fell from 3.4 percent in 2013 to 1.7 percent in 2023, equal to a 50 percent decline. He said the drop in HIV infections and the increased willingness of people living with HIV to join treatment and care services in the region is the result of the efforts of THPS in collaboration with stakeholders and the Government to build understanding, an enabling environment and community awareness. "Currently, many service recipients are in good health and are continuing to build our nation through various activities. Had there not been treatment as was the case in past years, many would be spending much of their time in bed suffering from illnesses," said Dr Ndossi.

a1088.speaker: Dk Frederick Ndossi, Director of Treatment and Care Services at THPS
a1088.speech: Said the 40 motorcycles, worth more than Sh141 million, were provided through the 'Afya Hatua' project implemented by THPS with funding from the US President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (Pepfar) through the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). He said they will be distributed to HIV treatment and care centres and clinics in the councils of Buhigwe (5), Kakonko (4), Kasulu (9), Kibondo, Kigoma (2) and Uvinza (11). "These motorcycles aim to enable essential HIV-related services, including transporting HIV viral load (HVL) test samples to the laboratories," said Dr Ndossi. He also said they will enable follow-up of clients who missed clinic appointments and encourage adherence to services, follow up on reports and contact tracing of sexual partners so that they can be reached by HIV testing services, and support community services such as the distribution of drugs that reduce the risk of HIV infection (PrEP) and the promotion of condom use.

a1088.speaker: Thobias Andengenye, Kigoma Regional Commissioner
a1088.speech: Speaking after receiving the motorcycles, urged health service providers at treatment and care centres in the region to respect the purpose for which the support was given, warning that those who divert them to other uses will not be overlooked. "The aim of these motorcycles is to build a friendly environment for the provision of treatment and care services for people living with HIV, so I urge service providers to use them to reach the vulnerable who need services delivered to them and who cannot afford to reach the centres," said Andengenye.

a1088.speaker: Dk Damas Kayera, Kigoma Regional Medical Officer
a1088.speech: Supported Andengenye's statement, saying he believes that after health service providers have been handed these motorcycles, they will fight and reduce HIV infections in the region from the current 1.7 percent to zero (0) percent by 2030.

a1095.speaker: Bill Gates, Co-Chair of the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation
a1095.speech: "There's no tradeoff where if you take less foreign aid you get more trade, those two things exist absolutely separately. Trade terms for Africa are actually in almost every case extremely favorable," stated during a conference call with African journalists ; stated that for the United States the African Growth and Opportunity Act gives Africa the lowest tariffs for trade ; "The key is to raise up the health and education and infrastructure and the quality of governments in Africa so that there's more output, high quality output. And, yes, over time growing the economies of the African countries, including through trade, growing the private sector, will be key to them achieving middle income status and being self-sufficient. But the foreign aid is helpful to that because the key thing is, you've got to get the health and nutrition and education up to a very high level to drive the economic growth at full speed."

a1095.speaker: Bill Gates, Co-Chair of the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation
a1095.speech: "Of course, Ethiopia has a plan where they're growing the infrastructure. They're improving the health. They're improving the farming output. And that over a 20-year period will move Ethiopia up to a kind of middle income status. And then probably the foreign aid will go and focus on countries that are not as far along."

a1095.speaker: Bill Gates, Co-Chair of the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation
a1095.speech: Underlined that when looking at malaria bed nets or vaccines for pneumonia or diarrhea or certain kinds of expertise, like the partnership the Foundation has had in Ethiopia with the Agricultural Transformation Agency, the benefits there have been strong ; "And, of course, in agriculture that becomes private sector and over time, as the livestock is more productive, as the seeds are more productive, that does result in trade. So in agriculture it is a direct connection to improving trade results. In the case of health, there's no direct financial payback, but it's those healthy kids going to school that will be key to the future economic growth."

a1095.speaker: Bill Gates, Co-Chair of the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation
a1095.speech: Speaking on the issue of unemployment among the youth on the continent, stated that there are appropriately expectations by those youth that the government will provide the stability, the food, the education and economic opportunity, and that it's a big enough population bulge that that won't be easy to do ; "Of course, this challenge was faced in the past by China and India and many Asian countries that managed both in agriculture and manufacturing and services to have good enough health of the population, and good enough education that they, both the domestic and the export market, were able to create that employment. Usually what happens is you raise the productivity in the agricultural sector and create value-added jobs in agriculture. You also have migration into the cities. So then in the cities you have to create in services and manufacturing quite a bit of new jobs."

a1095.speaker: Bill Gates, Co-Chair of the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation
a1095.speech: "There's a partnership between Ethiopia and UNIDO that's fairly unique in terms of looking at bringing factories, including a number of Chinese and other factories. And, of course, there's been a lot of work to build the infrastructure, like the rail and road connections through Djibouti. So as the country gets the increased electricity and improved infrastructure, there should be some opportunity for Ethiopia in particular to follow a Vietnamese-like model. But a ton of things need to work very well for that to happen in terms of the education quality, and the infrastructure quality, and the predictability of the government policies."

a1245.speaker: 2022 Lancet report on health systems performance
a1245.speech: Ranking health systems performance using healthcare access and quality placed Nigeria at 142 out of 195 countries, right in the basement.

a1245.speaker: President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s proposed 2025 budget
a1245.speech: Allocates only 5.18 per cent (N2.48 trillion) to healthcare, falling short of the 15 per cent target set by the Abuja Declaration.

a1351.speaker: Hassan Houmed Ibrahim, Djibouti's Minister Delegate for Trade
a1351.speech: Said that setting up a standardization system will make it possible to exploit the commercial opportunities of regional and international standardization for the Republic of Djibouti, to regulate and/or set rules for the domestic market on the basis of normative references, to combat unfair competition and fraud and to develop national production, to ensure the protection of health, and the safety of consumers' goods and services.

a1351.speaker: Standing Committee on Legislation and General Administration of Djibouti's National Assembly
a1351.speech: Found the minister's argument convincing and issued a favourable opinion with a view to the adoption of the bill at the next public session of the National Assembly.

a1473.speaker: Bill Gates, Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist
a1473.speech: pledged on Thursday to give away almost his entire personal wealth in the next two decades and said the world's poorest would receive some $200 billion via his foundation at a time when governments worldwide are slashing international aid ; said he was speeding up plans to divest his fortune and close the Gates Foundation on December 31, 2045 ; "People will say a lot of things about me when I die, but I am determined that 'he died rich' will not be one of them," he wrote in a post on his website ; "There are too many urgent problems to solve for me to hold onto resources that could be used to help people."

a1473.speaker: Bill Gates, Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist
a1473.speech: hit out at Elon Musk, accusing him of "killing the world's poorest children" with huge cuts to the United States aid budget: "The picture of the world's richest man killing the world's poorest children is not a pretty one," Gates told the Financial Times.

a1473.speaker: Bill Gates, Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist
a1473.speech: In an implicit rebuke to Trump's slashing of aid since returning to office in January, Gates' statement said he wanted to help stop newborn babies, children and mothers dying of preventable causes, end diseases like polio, malaria and measles, and reduce poverty ; "It's unclear whether the world's richest countries will continue to stand up for its poorest people," Gates added, noting cuts from major donors including Britain and France alongside the United States, the world's biggest donor ; said that despite the foundation's deep pockets, progress would not be possible without government support ; praised the response to aid cuts in Africa, where some governments have reallocated budgets, but said that as an example polio would not be eradicated without U.S. funding.

a1473.speaker: Bill Gates, Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist
a1473.speech: "I have come a long way since I was just a kid starting a software company with my friend from middle school," he said ; said the foundation will close after it spends around 99% of his personal fortune, and expects the foundation to spend around $200 billion by 2045, with the final figure dependent on markets and inflation.

a1473.speaker: Bill Gates, Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist
a1473.speech: "I hope other wealthy people consider how much they can accelerate progress for the world's poorest if they increased the pace and scale of their giving, because it is such a profoundly impactful way to give back to society," Gates wrote.

a1583.speaker: Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) studies
a1583.speech: Show that increase in firm-level innovation spending raises productivity over time.

a1665.speaker: François Ango Ndoutoume, 4th Vice-President of the Pan-African Parliament
a1665.speech: Welcomed the AU Media Fellows to PAP which he described as the home of the African people. He further referred to the role of the PAP's mandate to ensure the full participation of African peoples in the economic development and integration of the continent. "The mandate of the PAP as a representation of the peoples of Africa cannot be implemented without engaging and involving citizens and civil society. The media, therefore, remains the most effective tool to achieve this objective." He highlighted the critical role the media plays in enhancing active citizen engagement, explained that the PAP depends on journalists to inform the public about its work and that covering the continental Parliament requires an understanding of its origin, mandate and rules of procedure, and finally called on the media to regain control of the editorial line and the media coverage dedicated to Africa, as it is the only way to counter negative narratives about the continent.

a1665.speaker: Leslie Richer, African Union Director for Information and Communication
a1665.speech: Said cross border collaborative journalism being shaped through the AU Media Fellowship positions media outlets and journalists across Africa to own the narrative of the continent. "From your study trip in Germany, Ethiopia and now in South Africa, this connecting of thoughts will help not only to do your work better, but also as journalists you are creating a network, you are actually better able to address the issues on the continent and to create narratives that we want. A balance narrative of developments on the continent, one that is a clear representation of who we are but one that speaks of the situation that we find ourselves in." ; "We started this programme so that you can start realizing that you're not in competition with each other. There's a bigger challenge for us because we do not even collaborate as journalists, and that must change. So that's the role the African Union has to play, to bring media houses and journalists together." ; "the two organizations have a common goal of ensuring top-quality, balanced narrative on the continent, which will result in equally high-calibre reportage and for us, a crucial step towards achieving this is to provide the fellows with the capacity to deliver through such interactions and tours."

a1665.speaker: Dr. Dinesh Balliah, Acting Director of the Centre of Journalism at Wits University
a1665.speech: Shed light on the constantly changing needs of media audiences in Africa. She focused on how the needs of media consumers in Africa are fast changing, which calls for new approaches in the media industries in Africa. She said, "The media ecosystem is changing, and thus the curriculum of journalism has to improve to meet the dynamic ever-changing needs of the audiences. Today, we give assignments to students and we instruct them to present them in different formats like podcasting, data visualization etc."

a1665.speaker: Naeemah Dudan, Producer at Seen.tv
a1665.speech: Listed ways of getting funders and donors to support media work. She said that media personalities should find better approaches to donors and mentioned that good proposals for any idea are the key to persuading donors.

a1665.speaker: Tiffany Jackson-Zunker, Deputy Director for the US Africa Regional Media Hub
a1665.speech: Reiterated the United States' commitment to working with African media to include and elevate African voices in the most consequential global conversations. "The role of the media in a democracy is critical and our hub's primary objective is to support journalists, specifically those on the African continent by providing resources on U.S.-Africa policy, opportunities to engage with U.S. officials, and responding to queries from media representatives, the journalists who work with us have more tools at their disposal to write the stories their audiences want and need."

a1665.speaker: Sithembile Ntombela, Acting Chief Executive Officer of Brand South Africa
a1665.speech: Took the AU Media Fellows through the concept of nation branding, saying Africans must accept and embrace the Continent's uniqueness. "We have to recognize the uniqueness of each and every country's offering and package it in a way that complements each other in grabbing the attention of the world so that Africa becomes better. The important thing about the concept of branding Africa is the alignment and our intentions for the development and positive impact of social and economic benefit of all of us in Africa." She concluded her remarks by commending the African Union for being instrumental in taking leadership and being a facilitator of concepts and programmes that promote regional integration like the AU Media fellowship.

a1691.speaker: Washington / the White House (stated objectives of Massad Boulos's African tour)
a1691.speech: The other objective of this visit by the White House's Africa man is to "promote US private sector investment in the region" ; the tour is meant to "advance efforts towards a lasting peace" in eastern DRC.

a1691.speaker: Washington / the United States
a1691.speech: Washington does not hide its desire to provide assistance in securing this part of the DRC in return for easy access to the rare minerals that constitute the wealth of this vast Central African country.

a1691.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a1691.speech: Clearly made his support for Volodymyr Zelensky conditional on an agreement on the future exploitation of Ukraine's mineral wealth.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said many factors contribute to the rise of Lassa Fever but that climate change is a key contributor: the disease is transmitted by a particular rat common in some parts of the country, which explains the hot spots, and the virus is found in these animals, which act as reservoirs and may show no signs of illness while transmitting to people.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said the influence of climate change occurs in the hot seasons, when farmers start clearing bushes and deforestation kicks off, destroying the rats' natural habitats so that they are displaced and take refuge in people's homes; said that when rainfall delays or there is a shortfall it prolongs the window for human-rat contact, contributing to a rise in new cases during the dry season, and that delayed rainfall and droughts have been attributed to climate change.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said the disease peaks between December and May, "so we are in the season right now. That's why it's always good to start alerting people months before this season."

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said a major factor in rodent-to-human transmission is farmers' agricultural practices, as grains such as guinea corn and maize are spread out to dry and rats drop faeces, urine or saliva on them, infecting people who consume them without cooking properly; said poor sanitation also aids transmission, as communities with unsanitary waste disposal systems are more likely to have rats invade homes and contaminate food items.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said one of the easiest ways to avoid infection is to cultivate a culture of hand washing with soap and water, which also prevents transmission to others, and that hygiene is very important; advised that homes with leakages or holes where rats can enter should block all openings so that the rodents return to their natural habitat.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said Lassa Fever was previously a seasonal disease but now occurs throughout the year, with a peak in the dry season which may be extended for longer periods in parts of the country; said that during drought the rats' natural habitat is destroyed even more and they spend more time in homes, whereas during the rainy season vegetation gives them cover, which is why the disease is not common then.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said meningitis peaks during the hot season, cholera is all year round, COVID is heightened during the cold season, Mpox is not so seasonal, measles is all year round and mostly affects children, and flu occurs in the cold season; said the NCDC is managing about eight outbreaks, with the worst being heavy metal poisoning in Sokoto and Zamfara, the cause of which is still not certain and is being studied.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said Lassa Fever is a zoonotic disease dealt with under the One Health platform, combining the efforts of health, environment, agriculture and livestock agencies, with environment officials handling sanitation messaging and animal authorities working on reducing rodent populations in hotspot communities, though research views differ on rodent control because disturbing one part of the ecosystem might create another problem.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said poor personal and environmental hygiene remains a problem and that proper waste disposal and handwashing would reduce transmission.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said Lassa Fever is treatable but becomes severe when it develops into hemorrhagic fever with bleeding, kidney failure and risk of death; said the NCDC prioritised sensitising health care workers on symptoms so patients can be directed to facilities that can treat them, but people present late, and that not all facilities are equipped to treat severe Lassa Fever, which is why the agency supplies dialysis machines to some tertiary facilities.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Confirmed that most of the people who have died presented late: "This is why we keep saying, once you start noticing the signs, get yourself to the hospital. The doctors and health care workers know what to do. The idea is, get your treatment early enough to prevent complications."

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said Lassa Fever affects everyone but people between the ages of 18 and 45 are most vulnerable because they are the most mobile and active group, and that farmers and people who frequent farmlands are highly susceptible.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said the NCDC has an existing partnership with state and local governments, which know areas without facilities, and that it is not the NCDC's responsibility to create care systems there but to support and assist; said the agency conducts public awareness and enlightenment nationally and sends advisories to state and local governments to replicate in local languages for indigenous communities, providing materials, facilities and training for their staff.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said Mpox is "a funny disease" whose full epidemiology is not yet understood and research is ongoing into why it resurfaced and what is responsible for the spread; said it is considered zoonotic and is gotten from monkeys, that before Nigeria reported its first case in 2017 other African countries had started detecting cases so it could have been imported, but nothing is confirmed and it is not known whether it is endemic in Nigeria.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said Nigeria has the less dangerous clade II variant and is working to control the spread, while neighbouring Cameroon has the more dangerous clade I, which is concerning; said states close to the border area are being sensitised, the Nigeria Ports Health Authority is acting on people coming in, internal responses are being galvanised for early detection, and laboratories in those areas have been optimised, with a few able to characterise using the latest genomic sequences.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said Mpox is an infection transmitted by animals, likely endemic where those animals reside, and related to the agricultural practices of hunters and people who work with animals; said increased awareness is important and vulnerable groups, including those who hunt bushmeat such as rats and monkeys, must adopt good practices.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said it is not yet known which animal is infected in Nigeria and no link has been made, but monkeys are supposed to be reservoirs of these diseases and it is a high suspicion.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said vaccines cannot be used for everything and may give only short-lived protection, so childhood immunisation is essential but control methods addressing each mode of spread are also needed; said infection prevention and control, especially handwashing with soap and water, reduces the chances of contracting communicable diseases by over 40 per cent, and food should be cooked properly with clean hands; said Mpox skin rash can be treated with available drugs and the child will be fine, but late treatment can lead to a more serious superimposed bacterial infection, adding that no one has died of Mpox so far.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said IDP camps are inadequate, overcrowded and have poor sanitation so that diseases such as meningitis, Lassa Fever, cholera and Mpox thrive there; said support personnel should be present, there should be constant preparation for recurring emergencies such as annual flooding, state governments should prepare ahead to provide essential services including healthcare, and states should develop their own emergency preparedness capability because they cannot be totally dependent on the NCDC.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said sensitisation among this group is not adequate and more needs to be done as "health is everybody's business", particularly by state governments where most of these things occur, with the federal government helping states develop emergency preparedness capabilities.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said meningitis is caused by a bacterium that thrives in the hot season and spreads differently, which is why the disease is high in overcrowded settings and mass gatherings, affecting both children and adults, and that zero-dose children who are not immunised are more susceptible.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: Said the main problem with diphtheria is the lack of vaccine, which is part of the immunisation schedule but not available in the country, and that the NCDC is working with the Primary Healthcare Development Agency.

a1737.speaker: Jide Idris, Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC)
a1737.speech: On the dissolution of USAID, said "As a government, the earlier we stop relying on foreign assistance, the better for us. We need to take care of our situation here," adding that this is only possible if the economy is right, which is a major problem ; said the present administration is doing all it can within the economic conundrum, and that when the reduction was announced the federal government quickly released some money to address key areas of the health sector where it can bite harder ; said he hopes strategies developed by the Federal Ministry of Health will mitigate the impact, that the ministry is focused on creating an environment for local manufacturing of face masks, PPEs and vaccines, and that building local capacity will take a while but must be done: "The funding is not going to be enough right now, but this is a lesson for us to start."

a1810.speaker: Ministry of Livestock and Fisheries
a1810.speech: According to the Ministry, women in the sector are expected to see increased opportunities in seaweed farming, with the capacity to grow production from 4,000 tonnes to 10,000 tonnes annually.

a1810.speaker: George Kwandu, Director of Infrastructure and Development at the Ministry of Livestock and Fisheries
a1810.speech: Told this paper that Tanzania currently fails to fully capitalize on deep-sea fishing because much of the catch is taken by large foreign vessels or discarded due to a lack of transport facilities; the new port will address such shortfalls and allow fish not bound by contracts to be brought to Kilwa Masoko, where they can be processed and sold to traders, creating a more efficient and profitable supply chain ; "This fishing port will bring significant changes to the fishing sector in Tanzania. It will have the capacity to store 1,800 tonnes of fish at a time and accommodate ships measuring up to 35 meters."

a1810.speaker: Abdallah Ulega, Minister for Livestock and Fisheries
a1810.speech: Said, during the 8th Meeting of Ministers Responsible for Oceans, Inland Waters, and Fisheries of the Organization of African, Caribbean, and Pacific States (OACPS), that small-scale fishermen were playing a vital role in the country's fishing industry. He said that 95 percent of Tanzanian fishermen operate on a small scale basis, contributing significantly to both the economy and food security.

a1810.speaker: Samia Suluhu Hassan, President of Tanzania
a1810.speech: During the launch of the Kilwa Masoko port, mentioned plans for a similar facility in Bagamoyo to capitalize on the country's expansive coastline. She said the Kilwa port would open opportunities not only for fishermen but also for those involved in value-added processes, such as seaweed farming and fish processing ; "If Kilwa doesn't experience significant change after this project, we will need to evaluate where the problem lies, as the government is investing heavily to empower people and solve their challenges." She also discussed potential airport upgrades to facilitate the export of fish products from Kilwa, contingent on the port's success.

a1819.speaker: Moses Kunkuyu, Malawi Government spokesperson
a1819.speech: Has acknowledged the situation, stating that the government is implementing responsive measures.

a1833.speaker: Betchani Tchereni, Secretary to the Treasury of Malawi
a1833.speech: Provided further insight into the budget adjustments, explaining that funds were reallocated within existing votes to address key national priorities; said there is no real change in the value of the votes: "What we did in the budget was to move funds within votes and direct them to areas where we felt there was a need."

a1833.speaker: Betchani Tchereni, Secretary to the Treasury of Malawi
a1833.speech: Said that to address the financing gap government would borrow, primarily to support capital expenditures: "We prioritise borrowing for activities that will add value and potentially generate returns rather than for consumption."

a1833.speaker: Betchani Tchereni, Secretary to the Treasury of Malawi
a1833.speech: Pointed out that some budgetary reallocations were influenced by shifts in global funding trends, citing reductions in international support, including changes in United States Agency for International Development (USAid) funding to Malawi's health sector: "We still need to support persons living with HIV and strengthen the education sector using local resources."

a1833.speaker: Simplex Chithyola-Banda, Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs (budget statement)
a1833.speech: In his budget statement on Wednesday, outlined increases in several budget lines amounting to K52.2 billion, with an upward adjustment of K20 billion.

a1833.speaker: Fredrick Changaya, National Working Group on Trade Policy chairperson
a1833.speech: Urged local authorities to stick to the implementation strategies developed and financed in the 2025/26 National Budget to ensure that the resources generate a return on investment: "Malawi has strong policy ideas, but execution remains a challenge. Ensuring adherence to programme strategies is critical to achieving the intended impact."

a2012.speaker: UNHCR and London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) report, ‘A rapid assessment of the gender-based violence (GBV) situation and response in Cabo Delgado, Mozambique’
a2012.speech: Found evidence of widespread gender-based violence among people displaced by fighting in Cabo Delgado, including a case in which a community leader sexually abused a displaced woman and pressured her landlord into threatening her with eviction for filing a complaint with the police. The document said that women and girls who resist or file complaints are threatened with being removed from humanitarian assistance distribution lists, including support in food or other forms of assistance. Without giving figures, the study shows that abuses by rebel groups continue while people flee from conflict zones and in host sites.

a2012.speaker: Samuel Chakwera, UNHCR’s representative in Mozambique
a2012.speech: “We are concerned by these serious findings,” said in a statement ; “We must do more to respond to this crisis and support displaced families and their host communities.”

a2012.speaker: Samuel Chakwera, UNHCR’s representative in Mozambique
a2012.speech: Said the scenario reflects the lack of resources for humanitarian aid: “The crisis in Cabo Delgado faces a large gap in humanitarian support, a growing number of displaced people, shortage of funding, and a limited number of humanitarian agencies and structures to support often overstretched host communities” ; said it was necessary to have robust support for the 2022 programmes so that IDPs and their host communities do not face similar gaps in vital activities.

a2012.speaker: ACLED conflict registration project
a2012.speech: The conflict has led to more than 3,100 deaths, according to the ACLED conflict registration project.

a2012.speaker: Mozambican authorities
a2012.speech: More than 817,000 displaced people, according to Mozambican authorities.

a2012.speaker: Health in Humanitarian Crises Centre, LSHTM (@LSHTM_Crises), social media post
a2012.speech: “Join us today at 12:45 for an event on #GBV and #conflict. We will discuss the findings from our report with @UNHCRMozambique. Find out more” (December 9, 2021).

a2012.speaker: UNHCR Mozambique (@UNHCRMozambique), social media post
a2012.speech: “A study conducted by UNHCR + @LSHTM has found indications of widespread #GenderBasedViolence among #InternallyDisplacedPersons in #Moz. ‘A Rapid Assessment of the #GenderBasedViolence Situation and Response in Cabo Delgado’ was released today in Pemba.” (December 10, 2021).

a2049.speaker: A facilitator/seller of dissertations (anonymous)
a2049.speech: "If you already have a project done, it is 12,000 meticais with class sessions for immersion. Without the project, it is 15,000 meticais with the same support" ; explained that "the service includes a choice, a reformulation of the topic, complete structuring according to the institution's norms, introduction, development, conclusion and references, as well as formatting and possible corrections from the supervisor" ; sellers guarantee the originality of the works and provide proof of dissertations already successfully submitted, including to institutions such as Universidade Eduardo Mondlane (UEM), UNISCED and Universidade Católica de Moçambique.

a2049.speaker: Impasse Camblege, lawyer
a2049.speech: According to the lawyer, Mozambique still does not have specific legislation punishing the buying and selling of academic work; however, the Penal Code may allow interpretations that classify such acts as fraud and document forgery: "Universities have internal mechanisms against academic fraud, but these do not cover the third parties involved."

a2049.speaker: Eduardo Humbane, Pedagogical Director of UP-Maputo
a2049.speech: "This activity represents a serious threat to academic integrity."

a2049.speaker: Adão Matimbe, university professor
a2049.speech: "The practice undermines the country's development and harms the training of competent professionals."

a2049.speaker: Tércio Viola, Coordinator of the National Association of University Students of Mozambique (AEFUM)
a2049.speech: Explained that many students feel alone in the process of producing their final course work and seek outside help out of desperation.

a2049.speaker: Ministry of Education of Mozambique
a2049.speech: Confronted with the results of the investigation, the Ministry of Education said it was unaware of the scheme, but promised to open an inquiry to look into the situation.

a2093.speaker: Government of Zimbabwe (climate plan / Nationally Determined Contributions submitted to the UN)
a2093.speech: The government wrote in a new climate plan to cut emissions by 2035 submitted to the UN that the country is failing to meet its power demand; said the 1,050 MW Kariba South hydropower plant, which accounts for around 40 percent of Zimbabwe's installed electricity generation capacity, is operating at 185 MW because of water shortages; said it "intends to refurbish the old generating units at the coal-powered Hwange Power Station in 2025... raise its efficiency to around 40 percent and increase the capacity by 400 MW"; says it aims to reduce emissions by at least 40 percent per capita by 2035 compared to a business-as-usual scenario.

a2093.speaker: Kuda Manjonjo, just transition associate at Power Shift Africa (told Climate Home News)
a2093.speech: Said Zimbabwe is "a victim of circumstance"; said like other African countries, Zimbabwe is squeezed "in a very tight spot between providing energy but at the same time...not getting the financing that they need to actually transition" to clean energy sources; explained that at its worst two years ago, "we were going through 23 hours a day of no electricity"; "It would be very hard for any government in the world to justify not producing coal, which is there with the [power] plants, when people do not have electricity."

a2093.speaker: Kuda Manjonjo, just transition associate at Power Shift Africa
a2093.speech: Said this return to coal reflects a global failure to deliver just energy transitions in developing countries at a time when the US - the world's largest historic emitter - is pulling back from its climate finance commitments and is making a dash to extract more fossil fuels ; said Zimbabwe's plans are both "disheartening" and "disappointing", but it is "a symptom" of a bigger trend in which African countries are likely to be more "blatant" about relying on fossil fuels to meet their power needs than in previous rounds of UN climate plans.

a2093.speaker: Bloomberg (news report)
a2093.speech: Reported that almost all projects under a major US initiative to increase electricity access in Sub-Saharan Africa, known as Power Africa, are being terminated.

a2093.speaker: African leaders at the Mission 300 energy summit in Tanzania (joint statement)
a2093.speech: Adopted a joint statement citing gas as one of the energy sources needed to unlock "Africa's full energy potential".

a2093.speaker: Green groups on the continent part of the Don't Gas Africa campaign
a2093.speech: Described the statement as "ironical", adding that despite renewable energy's exponential growth globally, "the Mission 300 pledge seems to entrap Africans in a fossil gas-based system".

a2093.speaker: Daniel Sithole, director of the Zimbabwe-based Green Shango Environment Trust (told Climate Home)
a2093.speech: Said this "vicious cycle" of climate shocks leading to more fossil fuel use, which in turn worsens climate impacts, is inevitable without more climate finance reaching developing countries; said that without necessary support, "short-term economic advantages of fossil fuels will outweigh the long-term benefits of renewable energy" for most African countries; added that unless there is a concerted global effort to provide transition financing tailored to the unique contexts of African nations, the pursuit of fossil fuels will continue to provide a "short-term solution to immediate economic challenges".

a2121.speaker: Office of the President of Nigeria (statement)
a2121.speech: Said the Federal Executive Council, presided over by President Bola Tinubu, discussed on Monday the impact of the Trump policies, particularly regarding HIV, tuberculosis, and malaria funding, and that the meeting set up a multi-ministerial committee including representatives from the Ministries of Finance, Health, Defense, and Environment, as well as the Governors' Forum, tasked with developing a transition and sustainability plan to mitigate potential funding disruptions of health programmes in Nigeria.

a2121.speaker: Muhammad Pate, Nigerian Minister of Health
a2121.speech: "This administration is committed to ensuring that those receiving treatment do not experience interruptions" ; "We appreciate the US government's contributions over the years and remain committed to a constructive partnership while strengthening Nigeria's healthcare system with domestic resources."

a2121.speaker: Muhammad Pate, Nigerian Minister of Health
a2121.speech: Said the N4.8 billion emergency funding to procure 150,000 HIV treatment packs, part of the Presidential Treatment Programme, aims to ensure uninterrupted care for People Living with HIV in Nigeria while the government strategises on long-term sustainability, and emphasised that the decision reinforces Nigeria's commitment to reducing dependence on foreign aid: "This is an important signal that the federal government is committed to ensuring that life-saving treatments remain accessible, despite the changing dynamics in external support."

a2121.speaker: Premium Times (earlier report)
a2121.speech: Reported how a rash of foreign policies by the Trump administration could affect healthcare in Nigeria in areas like tackling HIV and vaccination.

a2121.speaker: National Agency for the Control of AIDS (NACA)
a2121.speech: Recently pledged to intensify domestic resource mobilisation strategies to ensure ownership and sustainability of the country's HIV/AIDS response.

a2121.speaker: Federal Executive Council (FEC) of Nigeria
a2121.speech: According to the FEC, the Human Capital Opportunities for Prosperity and Equity (HOPE) initiative, backed by the World Bank, aims to improve governance and primary healthcare services, with a total funding package of $1 billion.

a2407.speaker: National Charter of Eritrea (adopted February 1994, Nakfa)
a2407.speech: Outlines Eritrea’s aspirations to build a prosperous, unified, and just nation, where citizens can fulfil their potential in a peaceful, healthy, and sustainable environment; the objectives of the Charter align closely with the SDGs and Agenda 2063 and, in many respects, anticipated them by decades.

a2407.speaker: Eritrea (official national position)
a2407.speech: Eritrea does not reject international partnerships; it insists that they be genuine, equitable, and complementary to national priorities. Assistance that is time-bound and sought as a bridging gap is countenanced when it addresses specific, locally identified needs and strengthens national institutions, but it is rejected when it comes with suffocating conditionalities or risks fostering structural dependency. In Eritrea’s view, the fulcrum of development partnership must also be shifted to investment and trade, rather than on debilitating and perpetual hand-outs; the term “donors” is deemed as denigrating.

a2438.speaker: South African leaders (collectively)
a2438.speech: Interpret Trump’s decision to cut future funding to the country, on the basis of allegations of abuses and confiscation of land belonging to white people, as blackmail, and make themselves available to explain the land policy to the United States.

a2438.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
a2438.speech: Was the first to rebut Donald Trump’s criticism; on his social network on Monday denied the Republican’s accusations and made himself available to explain in detail the working of the land expropriation law in force in the country, acknowledging the importance of US support: “We are looking forward to engaging with the Trump administration over our land reform policy and issues of bilateral interest. We are certain that, out of these engagements, we will share a better and common understanding over these matters.”

a2438.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States
a2438.speech: Accuses the South African government of practising social and racial inequality and, with that, threatens to cut all funding to that country.

a2438.speaker: Gwede Mantashe, South African Minister of Mineral and Petroleum Resources
a2438.speech: Said during an event on Monday that his country and other African countries should begin to dissociate themselves from dependence on the US: “And I said, let us demobilise Africa. Let us withhold minerals from the US. If they don’t give us money, let us not give them minerals. But the reality is that they take our minerals, yet they say we are withdrawing the funding. No, we have minerals on the continent. So, my appeal is that Africa is the richest mining jurisdiction in the world. And this issue is an issue that we must internalise as a continent. Use it to our advantage. It is one of the things we can use to compete in the world. We cannot be the poorest continent.”

a2438.speaker: Julius Malema, leader of the Economic Freedom Fighters and member of the South African National Assembly
a2438.speech: Also criticised Trump’s remarks, which he said were offensive: “Donald Trump’s statement is offensive and undermines our sovereignty and is a reminder that our dependence on foreign aid and foreign direct investment surrenders us to the will of the imperialists who use money to dictate the economic and political course of Africa. We want to make it categorically clear to the President of the US that we will expropriate land without compensation and take legislative measures to do so and no threat will stop us.”

a2451.speaker: Disseta Zanze Traoré, president of the Association Solidarité et Développement Communautaire (ASDC)
a2451.speech: “Many of us did not even know the basic rules of sound management. We did not know that a bank account in the association's name is a transparency requirement, not an administrative formality.” ; “Before, we were moving forward blindly. Today, we better understand the importance of accounting for our decisions and our actions.”

a2451.speaker: Disseta Zanze Traoré, president of ASDC
a2451.speech: Insisted on the challenge of sustaining the gains: “We have learned a lot, but the challenge now is to continue relentlessly, to maintain this collective dynamic.”

a2451.speaker: Yerizon Kanko, president of the Association pour le Développement du Mouhoun et des Balé (ADMB)
a2451.speech: “This project came at just the right time to structure our commitment and professionalise our collective action.”

a2451.speaker: Yerizon Kanko, president of ADMB
a2451.speech: “It's a real revolution for our associations” ; “Thanks to social networks, we can finally show what we know how to do, reach new partners and market our products beyond Boromo.”

a2451.speaker: Yerizon Kanko, president of ADMB
a2451.speech: “What we learned goes beyond the training. It is a new way of envisaging our future, of seeing ourselves as actors capable of bringing solutions.”

a2451.speaker: Tiegna T. Jacques Armand, Director of Economic Action at the Regional Council and focal point of the PEG project in the Boucle du Mouhoun
a2451.speech: “We maximised our efforts in the secure areas so as not to abandon these populations. We worked closely with the humanitarian action services to identify displaced women, assess their needs and integrate them into our support systems.”

a2451.speaker: Tiegna T. Jacques Armand, focal point of the PEG project
a2451.speech: Considers that the key lies in the participatory and contextualised approach adopted by the project: “What made our approach strong was taking the time to listen to the women, to understand their realities and to build the solutions with them. This model can be transposed elsewhere, provided the tools and methods are adapted to each context.”

a2451.speaker: Tiegna T. Jacques Armand, focal point of the PEG project (interview)
a2451.speech: Explained that the project was implemented taking account of the region's security constraints, with efforts concentrated in host areas to support displaced people, with an emphasis on women and people with disabilities, through training, support for socio-professional integration and capacity building; a strategy was developed with the Directorate of Humanitarian Action, which at national level ensures that women and vulnerable people are included in support systems, and targeting based on identified needs, followed by individual interviews, made it possible to reach internally displaced women who are often barely visible in conventional systems.

a2480.speaker: Ambassador Richard Mills, U.S. Embassy and Consulate in Nigeria
a2480.speech: "We are pleased to know that this is a timely donation that will reach the affected areas across the country and those who are most vulnerable to mpox infection" ; he encouraged "the Government of Nigeria to continue to mobilize domestic resources to secure more vaccines to combat mpox."

a2480.speaker: Ambassador Richard Mills, U.S. Embassy and Consulate in Nigeria
a2480.speech: Regarding the vaccine's safety, confirmed: "Yes, the vaccine is safe. Safety tests have been conducted during clinical trials, and the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control reviewed the results of these trials before granting approval for the use of the vaccines in Nigeria."

a2548.speaker: Antonella D'Aprile, WFP Country Director in Mozambique
a2548.speech: “These dates will strengthen the diets of 100,000 people—especially women and children—and represent a meaningful gesture of solidarity from the people of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to the people of Mozambique”.

a2548.speaker: Mishaal Bin Shail, Acting Charge d'affaires of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to Mozambique
a2548.speech: “The gift of dates is a quiet yet powerful symbol of goodwill reflecting shared values, strengthening the bonds of friendship between our nations, and echoing a border spirit of care and solidarity that defines the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia's engagement with vulnerable communities”.

a2620.speaker: Rwandan government
a2620.speech: Said a first group of seven migrants has arrived in Rwanda as part of a deal to accept deportees from the United States.

a2620.speaker: Yolande Makolo, Rwandan government spokesperson
a2620.speech: “The first group of seven vetted migrants arrived in Rwanda in mid-August… Three of the individuals have expressed a desire to return to their home countries, while four wish to stay and build lives in Rwanda” ; said the first arrivals are “accommodated by an international organisation with visits by the International Organisation on Migration (IOM) and Rwandan social services.”

a2620.speaker: Yolande Makolo, Rwandan government spokesperson
a2620.speech: Said earlier this month that Kigali had agreed to the new scheme with Washington because “nearly every Rwandan family has experienced the hardships of displacement” ; added that those who arrive in Rwanda will be provided with training, healthcare and accommodation.

a2620.speaker: Rwanda (government statement of 5 August)
a2620.speech: Said it would accept up to 250 migrants from the United States, stating that it would have “the ability to approve each individual proposed for resettlement”.

a2620.speaker: IOM spokesperson
a2620.speech: Confirmed to AFP they had visited the newly arrived migrants to “assess their basic needs”. They did not give any further details.

a2620.speaker: Rwandan activist (anonymous)
a2620.speech: Said the deal came down to money and political influence: “Accepting these deportees also gives Rwanda an advantage in the ongoing peace negotiations regarding the conflict in DRC.”

a2620.speaker: Trump administration
a2620.speech: Has defended third-country deportations as necessary, since the home nations sometimes refuse to accept them.

a2620.speaker: Rights experts
a2620.speech: Have warned the arrangements risk breaking international law by sending people to nations where they face the risk of torture, abduction and other abuses.

a3229.speaker: Diplomatic sources (anonymous)
a3229.speech: Say President Irro used the meeting to offer assurances that Somaliland's bid for international recognition and its expanding geopolitical outreach would not come at the expense of Djibouti's interests.

a3229.speaker: Rashid Abdi, Horn of Africa expert at Nairobi-based Sahan Research
a3229.speech: "Djibouti was his first choice because it is an important neighbour with whom Hargeisa has a fraught relationship at the moment" ; "Irro made a good choice to visit Djibouti first and to seek to reassure the Red Sea State it has nothing to fear from Somaliland's rising international profile, a win for Somaliland does not equate to a loss for Djibouti."

a3229.speaker: Analysts
a3229.speech: Say the visit reflects a pragmatic recalibration of Somaliland's foreign policy, aimed at defusing regional anxieties and positioning Hargeisa as a cooperative actor in the geopolitics of the Red Sea corridor.

a3262.speaker: Dorothea von Boxberg, CEO of Brussels Airlines
a3262.speech: Extended her greetings and congratulations to the participants.

a3262.speaker: Marjolein Six, Country Manager Liberia, Brussels Airlines
a3262.speech: "At Brussels Airlines, we are committed not only to serve Liberia as an airline, with regular flights between Monrovia and Brussels. We want to go further. We want to be partners for the Liberian people. Learning to read and to write is for life. By partnering-up with read-to-succeed, we can plant a seed for many young Liberian people that will allow them to blossom for a very long time."

a3262.speaker: Ama Harris, Rosetta Steps Education Foundation
