a3262.speech: "Our organization is founded on the belief that education is a human right and the best means of combating inequality, poverty, and discrimination. Less than half of Liberians are literate. Inspired by the legacy of one of the country's most dedicated educators, Rosetta Benson, we consider it our mission to empower and educate as many Liberian youth and families in need as we can, and we're happy to do this with the support of Brussels Airlines and help alliance."

a3336.speaker: U.S. Agency for International Development in Liberia (USAID) and the Government of Liberia
a3336.speech: Have officially announced the launch of the Local Health Solutions (LHS) activity, a five-year initiative aimed at strengthening Liberia's health system, designed to improve the delivery of affordable, equitable, and high-quality health care services by fostering local leadership and supporting local organizations to take the lead in health systems strengthening, and focusing on promoting inclusive governance structures, strengthening supply chain management, enhancing data use, and improving the quality of services, including maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health; malaria services; and laboratory and disease surveillance systems.

a3336.speaker: Mark Toner, U.S. Ambassador to Liberia
a3336.speech: "This initiative goes beyond healthcare - it's about building resilience and ensuring that communities have the leadership and tools they need to thrive" ; "The United States is proud to work alongside Liberia to improve the quality of health for all, particularly in the most underserved areas."

a3535.speaker: Ilse De Boer, Deputy Medical Coordinator for Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) in South Sudan
a3535.speech: Wrote that the cholera epidemic is “a symptom of South Sudan’s deepest vulnerabilities: systemic neglect, incessant violence, and a fragile, underfunded healthcare system, resulting in significant service delivery gaps and lack of proper response,” and that “the scale of the outbreak is the result of a slow, underperforming and uncoordinated response – which has been a challenge since it began” ; asked why, one year after the outbreak was declared, “we are still fighting a preventable enemy that has already stolen over 1,500 lives and sickened over 93,000 people.”

a3535.speaker: Ilse De Boer, Deputy Medical Coordinator for Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) in South Sudan
a3535.speech: Said that as Deputy Medical Coordinator she was directly involved in leading MSF’s medical response, whose priority was setting up Cholera Treatment Units (CTUs) and Centres in Renk, Malakal, Ulang, Bentiu and Juba, expanding rapidly to numerous other areas “allowing us to treat more than 35,000 people.”

a3535.speaker: Ilse De Boer, Deputy Medical Coordinator for Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) in South Sudan
a3535.speech: Said the public healthcare system depends almost entirely on external support, with the government allocating less than two per cent of its budget to health, and that “the withdrawal of support from major donors—including USAID—has forced the closure of some health facilities, eliminating crucial lifelines” ; noted that in Bentiu “we witnessed how the reduction in funding to organisations that run water and sanitation and primary healthcare have left major gaps in the response, leaving people at risk while desperately searching for care.”

a3535.speaker: Ilse De Boer, Deputy Medical Coordinator for Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) in South Sudan
a3535.speech: Said the influx of more than 1 million people fleeing Sudan since April 2023, equivalent to 10 per cent of South Sudan’s population, has increased the burden on limited services at a time of reduced services due to funding cuts, with transit camps in Renk hosting more than three times their capacity, creating conditions that also drive waterborne diseases such as hepatitis E.

a3535.speaker: Ilse De Boer, Deputy Medical Coordinator for Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) in South Sudan
a3535.speech: Said “perhaps the cruellest obstacle is the pervasive violence, insecurity and attacks on healthcare,” citing fighting in Ulang in March 2025 that forced tens of patients, including more than 30 admitted for cholera treatment, to flee the MSF hospital, which was later permanently closed because of looting, and stated that since the start of 2025 MSF has been directly targeted in more than eight attacks, closing another hospital in Old Fangak in Jonglei state and reducing or suspending activities in others, cutting hundreds of thousands of people off from healthcare.

a3535.speaker: Ilse De Boer, Deputy Medical Coordinator for Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) in South Sudan
a3535.speech: Urged that “the government needs to step up and take its responsibilities to take care of its people,” including scaling up emergency preparedness and response capacities and prioritising service delivery in hot spot locations ; said “the international community must provide renewed humanitarian and development support, not only to try and close the massive gaps left by recent funding cuts but also to ensure a more effective humanitarian response with the limited resources that remain,” including sustainable water and sanitation programmes and widespread vaccination for cholera and hepatitis E ; and said “all parties to ongoing conflict must respect international humanitarian law and guarantee safe access to people in need,” warning that without this fundamental shift “new outbreaks will continue to occur, condemning the people of South Sudan to a bleak future of avoidable suffering.”

a3535.speaker: Eye Radio (Editor’s Note)
a3535.speech: Noted that “the views expressed in the above articles, as published by Eye Radio, are entirely those of the writer. Any claims made are the responsibility of the author, not Eye Radio’s.”

a3778.speaker: Elon Musk, billionaire entrepreneur and former head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)
a3778.speech: Made a stunning accusation, posted directly on X: that Trump was connected to convicted sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein and that he was on the Epstein list of powerful and politically connected global tycoons, politicians and business moguls who were allegedly involved in orgies and the sexual exploitation of women and underaged girls.

a3778.speaker: Elon Musk, billionaire entrepreneur and former head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)
a3778.speech: Denounced Trump’s legislative centerpiece, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, calling it “a disgusting abomination.”

a3778.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a3778.speech: Retaliated by proposing the termination of federal subsidies and contracts with Musk’s companies, including SpaceX and Tesla.

a3778.speaker: Insiders (anonymous)
a3778.speech: Suggested that Trump’s exclusion of Malawi from a proposed travel ban expansion widened the rift between the two oligarchs.

a3834.speaker: Bayo Onanuga, Special Adviser to the President on Information and Strategy
a3834.speech: In one of the statements he signed and issued on behalf of President Tinubu, stated that Vice President Kashim Shettima had been “ordered” by the president to proceed to London to bring back the corpse of President Buhari to Nigeria for burial.

a3834.speaker: Sam Omatseye, President Tinubu’s long-term private media adviser, in his article “Anti-climax”
a3834.speech: Described the late President Buhari as a man “who loved himself too much to love Nigeria enough. He loved his faith too much to open his heart out of his prejudices.” ; said of Buhari that “He was loved by both cow and man. He did less for man than cow, but cows never had a way of gratitude known to man, except men like him, perhaps.”

a3834.speaker: Colonel Martin Adamu, Buhari’s sector commander during the Nigerian civil war
a3834.speech: Disclosed to the team that met him in Jos in the course of background research on the late president that Buhari, as a young army officer and his Adjutant, was one of the first in the line of fire when the Nigerian civil war erupted in the border town of Gakem in the present Cross River State.

a3906.speaker: Camp residents, Kakuma Refugee Camp
a3906.speech: Say living conditions have sharply declined, with many struggling to access basic necessities.

a3906.speaker: A refugee from South Sudan in Kakuma (anonymous)
a3906.speech: Lamented: “This is what they are using to measure beans and oil. Another one is for rice. And this is supposed to last a whole month. If you have no other source of income, is this enough?” he asked.

a3906.speaker: World Food Programme (WFP)
a3906.speech: Announced on Monday that it is closing its office in South Africa, citing ongoing cuts in foreign aid from the U.S. under President Donald Trump's administration.

a3906.speaker: Mama Kayembe, Congolese refugee
a3906.speech: Voiced her frustration: “People blame Trump for everything. Workers are not being paid, hospitals have no medicine, and now we have to pay school fees. We are tired.”

a3906.speaker: World Food Programme (WFP) (statement last December)
a3906.speech: According to the WFP, food rations in the camp have been at 45% of the minimum food basket due to resource constraints ; the WFP acknowledged that it had been struggling to meet the needs of refugees, warning that funding shortfalls had significantly impacted its ability to provide adequate food assistance.

a4105.speaker: General Michael Langley, head of AFRICOM
a4105.speech: has praised Morocco as an “exemplary partner,” highlighting its contributions to UN peacekeeping missions, its military training capabilities, and its logistical cooperation.

a4263.speaker: King Letsie III, monarch of Lesotho
a4263.speech: Warned ahead of a trip to Europe that Lesotho will suffer from Donald Trump's aid cuts and stands to lose up to 40,000 jobs if the US president cancels a trade pact granting duty-free access to the American market: "If the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) is terminated, it will have an immediate impact on the economy because it could mean the loss of jobs for 30 000 to 40 000 people," he told AFP in his palace in Matsieng ; "It's a worrying thing - but if it happens, we'll have to deal with it."

a4263.speaker: King Letsie III, monarch of Lesotho
a4263.speech: "I was a little bit upset," said of Trump's remark that Lesotho was a country "nobody has ever heard of" ; "We have enjoyed very warm relations with the US and the people," he said, vowing to use the publicity from Trump's mockery to promote the country known for its beautiful mountainous terrain.

a4263.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a4263.speech: Defended the cuts to Lesotho, saying it was a country "nobody has ever heard of."

a4263.speaker: US embassy in Lesotho
a4263.speech: Revealed that the US has committed more than US$630 million since 2006 to anti-HIV/AIDS efforts in Lesotho.

a4335.speaker: Filipe Nyusi, Mozambican Head of State
a4335.speech: Revealed that the Niassa Special Reserve, the country's largest conservation area, has recorded no cases of elephant poaching since 2018, and explained that this is due to investments, legal reforms and institutions established over the years: "The investments and legal reforms we have been carrying out in the conservation areas have brought a new dynamic and important gains for the reserve, namely human resources and the reduction of illegal activities, through the development of more rangers using motorised means, boats and aerial means." ; thanked the Defence and Security Forces for their contribution as well as the collaboration of the rangers ; said the increase in the number of partners and the "healthy coexistence of the different operators, alongside the government and the communities" also contributes to a healthy environment for the development of the reserve ; pointed to the use of technological devices as monitoring instruments.

a4335.speaker: Helen Pataki, Director of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) in Mozambique
a4335.speech: Endorsed Nyusi's remarks and said United States support for monitoring services played a leading role in reaching this milestone: "The support of the United States Government's Area Surveillance Programme made possible the monitoring and also the deployment of patrols, which led to a reduction in cases of illegal mining and logging in the Special Reserve, as well as contributing to zero elephant poaching rates since 2018." ; said preserving biodiversity is necessary at a time when the world faces challenges such as climate change and environmental degradation.

a4335.speaker: Afonso Madope, representative of the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS)
a4335.speech: Highlighted the leading role of the forces the Government deployed to the park in reducing poaching: "I wanted to highlight the special effort made by the government in allocating Defence and Security Forces that helped to halt the critical problem of elephant poaching, and today, thanks to that, we celebrate with pride and with a full mouth the non-existence of a single elephant killed by illegal activity in the Niassa Reserve." ; noted that eight million dollars a year are needed to guarantee the sustainability of the conservation area, and stressed that WCS, co-manager of the Reserve, invested with its partners approximately 40 million dollars from 2012 to 2023 in various projects, including the socio-economic development of communities living inside and around the Reserve.

a4362.speaker: Selma Ashipala-Musavyi, Namibian Minister of Trade and International Relations
a4362.speech: Says SADC must unite to bankroll its own development, as no one else will do it for them, a position Namibia will fervently advance during the 45th SADC Heads of State and Government Summit: “Regional projects benefit everyone, but they strain national budgets. We must fund our own development; nobody will do it for us.”

a4362.speaker: Selma Ashipala-Musavyi, Namibian Minister of Trade and International Relations
a4362.speech: Said Namibia’s push is not only about energy but also about adding value to agricultural products and minerals before they are exported: “Most of our mineral resources are going out in raw form. Value addition is key. The African Union has set a target of at least 20% value addition for all commodities leaving our continent. We must meet that target and more so that we create jobs at home.”

a4362.speaker: Selma Ashipala-Musavyi, Namibian Minister of Trade and International Relations
a4362.speech: Told this newspaper that the creation of the regional centre for renewable energy has been delayed because some member states have not yet ratified the agreement, and added that Namibia is also aiming to champion a shift toward regional self-reliance, with plans to fast-track the renewable energy centre, saying it will host and deepen industrial value chains ; “If we have to industrialise, we have to have energy. You can’t do that without energy. We are going to be advocating for ratification so that we can set up that centre.”

a4362.speaker: Selma Ashipala-Musavyi, Namibian Minister of Trade and International Relations
a4362.speech: Said that while Namibia is not currently part of SADC’s military mission in the DRC, it continues to make financial contributions and advocate for peace: “Peace in the DRC should concern everyone. We must ensure the territorial integrity and sovereignty of that country are fully respected.”

a4362.speaker: Selma Ashipala-Musavyi, Namibian Minister of Trade and International Relations
a4362.speech: Said the ‘Namib Declaration’, first adopted 15 years ago to strengthen regional drought and desertification responses, will be revived and used to mobilise international resources for resilience ; added that Namibia’s goals of energy integration, value addition and regional financing are closely aligned with the Secretariat’s call for deeper economic self-reliance and Madagascar’s vision for inclusive growth; and said Namibia is anticipating success that will mean turning these priorities into concrete outcomes from SADC by securing the renewable energy centre, launching the SADC Development Fund, and ensuring that industrialisation benefits every corner of the region.

a4362.speaker: Elias Magosi, SADC Executive Secretary (opening remarks to the Council of Ministers)
a4362.speech: Said SADC has mobilised US$194.5 million in 2024/25, plus US$12.3 million in the first four months of 2025/26 from partners – but implementing priority projects under the RISDP will require about US$624.5 billion; he urged the bloc to show tangible results and lean more on domestic resources to reduce exposure to fickle foreign aid ; underscored the importance of environmental protection and early warning systems in SADC’s strategy.

a4362.speaker: Rasata (Madagascar official)
a4362.speech: Called for joint action to address climate impacts such as droughts, cyclones, and threats to natural resources.

a4389.speaker: Fyawupi Mwafongo, Deputy Director for Disaster Response at the Department of Disaster Management Affairs (DoDMA)
a4389.speech: Stated that the first batch of 4,000 metric tons of maize is already on its way to various districts across Malawi ; “This is not just about maize; it is about giving hope. For many families, this maize will be the difference between having a meal and going hungry,” Mwafongo said, stressing that the government’s approach is both practical and compassionate.

a4389.speaker: Fyawupi Mwafongo, Deputy Director for Disaster Response at the Department of Disaster Management Affairs (DoDMA)
a4389.speech: “We are not only focused on providing food, but also ensuring that families have access to nutritious food,” Mwafongo stated. “This is a holistic approach to addressing hunger, and it involves collaboration with other stakeholders to ensure that the right food reaches the right people.”

a4389.speaker: Cosmas Peleka, Operations Director at the National Food Reserve Agency (NFRA)
a4389.speech: Said the agency has procured 83,000 metric tons of maize to distribute throughout the country, of which over 16,000 metric tons have already been delivered to DoDMA for distribution, with an additional 5,874 metric tons released to the Agricultural Development and Marketing Corporation (ADMARC) to help stabilize maize prices in the market ; “Food security is a top priority for the government, and we are using every available resource to ensure that no one goes hungry. This maize will help to stabilize prices and ensure that food is available and affordable for all Malawians,” Peleka explained.

a4389.speaker: President Lazarus Chakwera of Malawi
a4389.speech: In his recent speeches, has called for national unity and collective responsibility in addressing the food crisis, urging all Malawians to play an active role in supporting government efforts ; “We must all stand together in solidarity to ensure that no one in Malawi goes to bed hungry. This is a national effort, and together, we can ensure that every Malawian has access to food, especially during these challenging times.”

a4663.speaker: Bill Gates, Co-Chair of the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation
a4663.speech: Stated during a conference call with African journalists: “There's no tradeoff where if you take less foreign aid you get more trade, those two things exist absolutely separately. Trade terms for Africa are actually in almost every case extremely favorable” ; stated that for the United States the African Growth and Opportunity Act gives Africa the lowest tariffs for trade ; “The key is to raise up the health and education and infrastructure and the quality of governments in Africa so that there's more output, high quality output. And, yes, over time growing the economies of the African countries, including through trade, growing the private sector, will be key to them achieving middle income status and being self-sufficient. But the foreign aid is helpful to that because the key thing is, you've got to get the health and nutrition and education up to a very high level to drive the economic growth at full speed.”

a4663.speaker: Bill Gates, Co-Chair of the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation
a4663.speech: On Ethiopia: “Of course, Ethiopia has a plan where they're growing the infrastructure. They're improving the health. They're improving the farming output. And that over a 20-year period will move Ethiopia up to a kind of middle income status. And then probably the foreign aid will go and focus on countries that are not as far along.” ; underlined that when looking at malaria bed nets or vaccines for pneumonia or diarrhea or certain kinds of expertise, like the partnership the Foundation has had in Ethiopia with the Agricultural Transformation Agency, the benefits there have been strong: “And, of course, in agriculture that becomes private sector and over time, as the livestock is more productive, as the seeds are more productive, that does result in trade. So in agriculture it is a direct connection to improving trade results. In the case of health, there's no direct financial payback, but it's those healthy kids going to school that will be key to the future economic growth.”

a4663.speaker: Bill Gates, Co-Chair of the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation
a4663.speech: On youth unemployment: stated that there are appropriately expectations by those youth that the government will provide the stability, the food, the education and economic opportunity, and that it's a big enough population bulge that that won't be easy to do ; “Of course, this challenge was faced in the past by China and India and many Asian countries that managed both in agriculture and manufacturing and services to have good enough health of the population, and good enough education that they, both the domestic and the export market, were able to create that employment. Usually what happens is you raise the productivity in the agricultural sector and create value-added jobs in agriculture. You also have migration into the cities. So then in the cities you have to create in services and manufacturing quite a bit of new jobs.” ; “There's a partnership between Ethiopia and UNIDO that's fairly unique in terms of looking at bringing factories, including a number of Chinese and other factories. And, of course, there's been a lot of work to build the infrastructure, like the rail and road connections through Djibouti. So as the country gets the increased electricity and improved infrastructure, there should be some opportunity for Ethiopia in particular to follow a Vietnamese-like model. But a ton of things need to work very well for that to happen in terms of the education quality, and the infrastructure quality, and the predictability of the government policies.”

a4788.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a4788.speech: "For decades, our country has been looted, pillaged, and plundered by nations near and far, both friend and foe alike" ; said the 60 countries subject to additional "reciprocal" tariffs were the worst offenders.

a4788.speaker: Scott Bessent, US Treasury Secretary
a4788.speech: Said "more than 75" world leaders have reached out to the president to make deals and offer trade concessions.

a4788.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a4788.speech: Said on Tuesday that countries were "kissing my ass" and promising to do anything.

a4788.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a4788.speech: "Jobs and factories will come roaring back into our country...We will supercharge our domestic industrial base" ; has said for decades that tariffs are an effective way of rebuilding America's manufacturing base by shielding it from unfair foreign competition.

a4788.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a4788.speech: "I have great respect for President Xi of China, great respect for China, but they were taking tremendous advantage of us" ; on Wednesday said that he blamed past US leaders, not China, for the current trade dispute.

a4788.speaker: Scott Bessent, US Treasury Secretary
a4788.speech: Was quick to say that Trump's goal was to drop the hammer on the real villain, China: "They are the biggest source of the US trade problems, and indeed they are the problem for the rest of the world."

a4788.speaker: Karoline Leavitt, White House press secretary
a4788.speech: Said the president would be "incredibly gracious" if China reaches out to make a deal.

a4788.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a4788.speech: "Now it's our turn to prosper, and in so doing, use trillions and trillions of dollars to reduce our taxes and pay down our national debt, and it'll all happen very quickly" ; regularly touted during last year's presidential campaign that his proposed tariffs would bring in vast sums in new revenue.

a4788.speaker: Tax Foundation (nonpartisan) study
a4788.speech: Estimated that a 10% universal tariff would generate $2tn in new revenue over the next 10 years ; last year estimated that a 10% universal tariff would increase costs for American households by an average of $1,253 in its first year.

a4788.speaker: Bipartisan Policy Center
a4788.speech: According to it, the tax cuts Congress recently included in its non-binding budget blueprint would cost approximately $5tn over the next 10 years.

a4788.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a4788.speech: "Ultimately, more production at home will mean stronger competition and lower prices for consumers. This will be indeed the golden age of America."

a4788.speaker: Economists (consensus)
a4788.speech: The consensus among economists is that new tariffs will drive up consumer prices, as tariffs are tacked on to the price of imports and, eventually, when there is less competition for US-made products; economists also warn that lower-income Americans will be hardest hit.

a4936.speaker: Aden Duale, Kenyan Health Cabinet Secretary
a4936.speech: emphasized the government's investment in digital health systems designed to promote transparency, efficiency, and accountability in service delivery; highlighted integration, coordination, and value for money as guiding principles in implementing health reforms, noting that the Global Fund's priorities align closely with those of Gavi, PEPFAR, and national investments: "These efforts aim to strengthen laboratory networks, disease surveillance, and digital innovations from the community to the referral level."

a4936.speaker: Aden Duale, Kenyan Health Cabinet Secretary
a4936.speech: praised German partners for their crucial role in accelerating local vaccine production and research - key drivers of Kenya's health security and sustainability (discussions on the Kenya Biovax Institute, focusing on equipment sharing, technology transfer, and capacity development).

a4936.speaker: Aden Duale, Kenyan Health Cabinet Secretary
a4936.speech: affirmed that Kenya continues to meet its 20% co-financing requirement under Global Fund guidelines, committing USD 593.3 million under the Fifth Administration to sustain HIV, TB, malaria, and community health programs; reaffirmed the Ministry's commitment to national and global health goals, citing Kenya's progress in reducing new HIV infections and expanding access to life-saving antiretroviral therapy.

a5179.speaker: U.S. Government (statement)
a5179.speech: “The U.S. Government, through USAID and GiveDirectly, is implementing a direct cash assistance project aimed to reduce poverty in rural, disaster-prone farming communities. The communities involved were selected on the basis of need, in coordination with local officials, civil society, and the private sector. The project has no partisan or political affiliations. We strongly refute recent social media claims falsely linking this project to partisan activities.”

a5179.speaker: GiveDirectly (@GiveDirectly, social media post, December 3, 2024)
a5179.speech: “Help us reach all 650 families in need by giving today.”

a5251.speaker: Edgar Lungu, Zambia's Sixth President, Tonse Alliance chairperson and Patriotic Front (PF) president
a5251.speech: Said in a statement released on behalf of the alliance that the Tonse Alliance has announced a series of interim leadership appointments as the coalition finalizes its larger leadership structure, naming key figures to various national leadership roles and emphasizing their role in guiding and coordinating Tonse activities ; expressed confidence in the appointed individuals, stating that they will play a crucial role in shaping and coordinating the alliance's activities ; reaffirmed the coalition's commitment to unity under the national motto, "One Zambia, One Nation."

a5368.speaker: Health ministers from 11 AU member countries with high malaria burdens, and Jean Kaseya (joint declaration)
a5368.speech: Committed to accelerate efforts to reduce deaths from the disease; as part of the declaration, they agreed that "no one should die from malaria given the tools and systems available."

a5368.speaker: Jean Kaseya, Director-General of the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
a5368.speech: Says the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention "is ready to help develop a continental strategy for ending malaria in Africa by 2040"; and states: "let me be clear: investing in the fight to end malaria is not only a health and economic imperative; it is an act of justice."

a5532.speaker: Ajay Banga, World Bank President
a5532.speech: “These are the kinds of businesses that drive economies.” ; “Electricity isn’t just light, it’s a chance.” (in an interview with The Associated Press during a July visit to tour electrification projects)

a5532.speaker: Ajay Banga, World Bank President
a5532.speech: “Mozambique has the resources, gas, hydro, solar, and it’s already the biggest supplier of excess power to southern Africa.”

a5532.speaker: Ajay Banga, World Bank President
a5532.speech: Said this approach in Africa aims to move away from reliance on donors for high-impact projects: “Many shareholders, even in Europe, are reducing their overseas development assistance budgets because they have to divert the money to defense and their own needs. This is the way it is.”

a5532.speaker: Ajay Banga, World Bank President
a5532.speech: Said the project’s final cost is yet to be determined but estimated $5 billion to $6 billion.

a5532.speaker: World Bank (data)
a5532.speech: According to the World Bank, sub-Saharan Africa is home to 85% of the global population living without power.

a5532.speaker: Electricidade de Moçambique (EDM), state-run energy supplier
a5532.speech: Says it connected 563,000 homes in 2024 and plans to reach 600,000 this year.

a5532.speaker: Joaquim Ou-Chim, EDM chairman
a5532.speech: “Our country is quite big, and it’s not so easy to go everywhere with the national grid. So it’s off-grid solutions, mainly driven by solar.”

a5532.speaker: Evaristo Cumbane, energy consultant based in Maputo
a5532.speech: Said large projects like Cahora Bassa and Mphanda Nkuwa are important but stressed the need for smaller, local sources of energy: “We are talking about plenty of rivers, plenty of sunshine, plenty of wind, plenty of coastlines,” adding that “the real Mozambique is in rural, remote areas.”

a5532.speaker: Evaristo Cumbane, energy consultant based in Maputo
a5532.speech: Urged caution over Mozambique’s growing debt burden: “The World Bank is not a godfather, it is not god. The guy is here on business. These are not donations.”

a5532.speaker: Finance Ministry of Mozambique (figures)
a5532.speech: According to the Finance Ministry, a record $2.1 billion was spent in 2023 in debt service.

a5532.speaker: World Bank and the International Hydropower Association (estimate)
a5532.speech: Estimate that around 90% of Africa’s hydropower capacity is still unused.

a5532.speaker: Aurélio Arlindo, 38-year-old unemployed resident of a neighbourhood outside Maputo
a5532.speech: “It’s really coming. I am just waiting,” he said, and he hopes to open a cold drinks stall.

a5540.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5540.speech: “My administration is committed to strengthening our friendships in Africa through economic development efforts that benefit both the United States and our partners,” Trump said at a White House event with leaders from Gabon, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Mauritania and Senegal; said there was “tremendous wealth there and potential” in those nations and highlighted his efforts to drum up more deals with other economies in lieu of US foreign assistance ; “We’re shifting from aid to trade. In the long run this will be far more effective and sustainable and beneficial than anything else that we could be doing together.”

a5540.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5540.speech: Suggested he could exempt the assembled countries from his plans to impose heightened reciprocal tariffs beginning in August, saying the assembled leaders were “friends of mine now.”

a5540.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5540.speech: Urged the leaders to keep their remarks brief, saying he had to leave their gathering for another event: “Maybe we have to go quicker than this because we have a whole schedule.” Asked if he planned to visit the continent, the president demurred, saying he would like to plan a trip but needed “to see what the schedule is like.”

a5540.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5540.speech: Complimented the leader of Liberia on his speaking: “Where did you learn to speak so beautifully? Where were you educated? Where in Liberia? … Well, that’s very interesting. It’s beautiful English. I have people at this table can’t speak nearly as well.”

a5540.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5540.speech: Said he would encourage the countries to “make greater investments in defence, hopefully, of course, buying our equipment,” and said he would raise the issue of immigration as his administration ramps up deportations of undocumented migrants.

a5540.speaker: International Monetary Fund (data)
a5540.speech: According to the IMF, the five countries whose leaders are visiting the White House have a combined gross domestic product of only around $75 billion.

a5540.speaker: Government of Liberia (announcement)
a5540.speech: Ahead of the talks, Liberia’s government announced that it’s signed a $1.8 billion agreement with Ivanhoe Atlantic Inc., which will allow the US mining company to rehabilitate and use the country’s railway infrastructure to transport iron ore from neighbouring Guinea for export; the government also announced earlier this year it has deposits of critical minerals including lithium, manganese, cobalt and neodymium that it hopes will attract $3 billion of investment.

a5540.speaker: Noël Nelson Messone, Gabon’s ambassador to the US
a5540.speech: Said in an interview that Gabon is expecting to discuss potential investments in its minerals industry: “The president of the republic is keen to see Gabon’s natural resources processed locally to add value to the economy, diversify the economy and create jobs.”

a5540.speaker: Liberian Observer (news report)
a5540.speech: Reported last week that the Liberian government plans to lobby for US investment in its natural resources, including fisheries.

a5586.speaker: Horace Kashema, doctor in Goma
a5586.speech: “We are so overwhelmed, but we keep working and we hope that with the situation having calmed down a little, that will help us to work. But our supplies are going to run out soon. We do not have enough.”

a5586.speaker: Doctors of Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF)
a5586.speech: Warn of the worsening of injuries in an increasingly difficult environment.

a5586.speaker: Joseph Sangara, doctor and coordinator of the MSF project in Goma
a5586.speech: “In similar situations, we know that between 10 and 20% of cases are critical cases. These are complicated cases, and these are the ones we are seeing. There are skull injuries, chest injuries. It is difficult to manage.”

a5586.speaker: Virginie Napolitano, MSF emergency coordinator in Goma (via MSF International post on X, 1 February 2025)
a5586.speech: “Goma was cut off from the world, it was a total blackout” — she tells of a week of chaos in the city, and how MSF teams adapted to treat war-wounded people.

a5628.speaker: Aaron Motsoaledi, South African Health Minister
a5628.speech: Announced that the treasury has given R622 million of emergency funding to his department to prop up South Africa's HIV treatment programme.

a5628.speaker: South African health department
a5628.speech: Says the country needed roughly R2.8 billion after the Trump administration pulled the plug on financial support for HIV in February; the Pepfar budget for this financial year was just under R8 billion, but the department calculated it could fill the void with R2.8 billion if it trimmed extras and ruled out duplicate positions.

a5628.speaker: Kate Rees, co-chair of the 12th South African Aids Conference
a5628.speech: Said the best value from limited funds comes from getting really serious about giving people more than one way of getting their repeat prescriptions for antiretroviral (ARV) medicine (so-called differentiated service delivery).

a5628.speaker: Lynne Wilkinson, public health expert working with the health department on public health approaches to help people stay on treatment
a5628.speech: "People who interrupt their antiretroviral treatment are increasingly common, but so are people who re-engage, in other words start their treatment again after having stopped for a short period."

a5628.speaker: South African health department
a5628.speech: Says South Africa currently stands at 79% of people diagnosed with HIV being on treatment, against the UN's 95% target ; says South Africa will start rolling out six-month dispensing in August.

a5628.speaker: Kate Rees, co-chair of the 12th South African Aids Conference
a5628.speech: Says the way many health facilities are run makes the system too rigid to accommodate real-life stop and start behaviour, which means extra time and money are spent every time someone seemingly drops out of line and then comes back in, and also makes people unwilling to get back on board because the process is so inconvenient and unwelcoming.

a5628.speaker: Study by Rees and Wilkinson published in the Journal of the International Aids Society (2024)
a5628.speech: Results helped the health department to update the steps health workers should follow when someone has missed an appointment for picking up their medicine or getting a health check-up; data from three health facilities in Johannesburg showed that of the 2,342 people who came back to care after missing a clinic appointment, 72% showed up within 28 days of the planned date and most (65%) weren't more than two weeks late; of those who showed up more than four weeks after they were due, 13% made it within 90 days, and only one in 14 people came back later than this; seven out of 10 people who collected medication four weeks or more late had no worrying signs; 71% had fewer than 1,000 copies/mL on their last viral load results; close to three-quarters of people who turned up four weeks or more late said they had missed their appointment because of travelling, work commitments or family obligations.

a5628.speaker: Kate Rees, co-chair of the 12th South African Aids Conference
a5628.speech: "We often have excellent guidelines in place, built on solid scientific evidence, but they're not necessarily implemented well on the ground."

a5628.speaker: Yogan Pillay, the health department's former deputy director general for HIV and now head of HIV delivery at the Gates Foundation
a5628.speech: "The standard ways in which the public health system works mostly doesn't provide the type of support these patients need, as the resources required to provide such support is not available" ; "But with AI-supported digital health solutions and the high penetration of mobile phones, such support can now — and should be — be provided at low cost and without the need to hire additional human resources."

a5628.speaker: Kate Rees, co-chair of the 12th South African Aids Conference
a5628.speech: Notes: "But it's important to distinguish between showing up late and interrupting treatment."

a5628.speaker: Pepfar (definitions)
a5628.speech: Pepfar definitions say that a window of up to 28 days (four weeks) can be tolerated for late ARV pick-ups.

a5628.speaker: Research (unnamed)
a5628.speech: Research has shown that for many people who have been on treatment for a long time already, viral loads start to pass 1,000 copies/mL — the point at which someone could start being infectious again — about 28 days after treatment has truly stopped.

a5628.speaker: South African health department (current guidelines)
a5628.speech: Current health department guidelines, updated since the study and in part because of its results, say that a medicine pick-up point can hold on to someone's medicine for four weeks after their scheduled appointment.

a5628.speaker: Kate Rees, co-chair of the 12th South African Aids Conference
a5628.speech: "Most people don't need more adherence counselling; they need more convenience" ; explains that offering services that aren't necessary because of an inflexible process wastes resources, something a system under pressure can ill afford ; "With funding in crisis, we really have to prioritise [where money is spent]."

a5628.speaker: Kate Rees, co-chair of the 12th South African Aids Conference
a5628.speech: Says part of making cost-effective decisions about how to use budgets best is to offer differentiated care, meaning that "not every patient coming back after a missed appointment is treated the same way", and that health workers should look at how much the appointment date was missed as well as a patient's health status to decide what service they need.

a5628.speaker: Lynne Wilkinson, public health expert working with the health department
a5628.speech: Told Bhekisisa's Health Beat team in July that giving people who've been managing their condition well enough medicine to last them six months at a time can go a long way: "Getting 180 pills in one go reduces the number of clinic visits [only twice a year], which eases the workload on staff. But it also helps patients to stay on their treatment by cutting down on their transport costs in their own time off work." ; "But not everyone wants this," pointing out that experiences from other countries show that 50% to 60% of people choose six-monthly pick-ups.

a5628.speaker: Kate Rees, co-chair of the 12th South African Aids Conference
a5628.speech: Says it speaks to tailoring service delivery to patients' needs, rather than enforcing a one-size-fits-all system when more than one size is needed: "Facing funding constraints, we really need tailored service delivery to keep the [HIV treatment] programme where it is."

a5866.speaker: Mashood Lawal, pharmacist and member of the WHO Taskforce of Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) Survivors
a5866.speech: Explained that the various antibiotics he was prescribed were ineffective against the infection as the symptoms kept coming back ; "I was admitted in the hospital and administered several courses of expensive injectable antibiotics. But the infection persisted even after I survived COVID-19 and was discharged from the hospital" ; described his experience as horrifying, adding that the infection was finally resolved after a course of a reserve antibiotic.

a5866.speaker: "Ade", AMR survivor (name withheld)
a5866.speech: Said he had E. coli and didn't feel better with the several courses of antibiotics prescribed for him by his doctor, including amoxicillin and ciprotab ; said he was able to get better over time but added that doctors "could also help by requesting blood culture test soon enough to know which antimicrobials the infection is sensitive to."

a5866.speaker: Dr Emmanuelle Soubeyran, Director General of WOAH
a5866.speech: "Many of the life-saving drugs are dangerously losing their efficacy, which has devastating impacts not only on human health but also on livestock and the economy at large."

a5866.speaker: World Health Organisation (WHO)
a5866.speech: Says the misuse and overuse of antimicrobials in humans, animals and plants is one of the main drivers of AMR ; said some ways that everyone including the public, doctors, veterinarians and farmers can help stop antimicrobial resistance include keeping your hands clean and only taking antibiotics when prescribed.

a5866.speaker: Nigeria Centre for Disease Control (NCDC)
a5866.speech: According to the NCDC, antibiotics are widely used for the treatment of infections in humans and animals, however, the misuse of antibiotics leads to AMR ; data from the NCDC showed that AMR kills more people than malaria, HIV & TB.

a5866.speaker: Dr Tochi Okwor, Antimicrobial Resistance lead, NCDC
a5866.speech: Said the drivers of AMR in Nigeria include poor levels of AMR awareness among health workers, policy makers, and the general public, driven by overuse and misuse of antibiotics ; "Taking antibiotics when they're not needed, buying antibiotics without a prescription, using too many antibiotics in farming" ; also said other drivers are poor hygiene and sanitation in community, health facilities, farms, abattoirs, and limited surveillance systems for tracking.

a5866.speaker: Dr Tochi Okwor, Antimicrobial Resistance lead, NCDC
a5866.speech: "In Nigeria, 64,500 deaths attributable to AMR and 263,400 deaths associated to AMR."

a5866.speaker: Laxmikant Chavan, technical officer, AMR and coordinator - One Health, WHO Nigeria
a5866.speech: Explained that during Nigeria's outbreak of diphtheria, tests revealed that at least two to three antibiotics were not working against the disease.

a5866.speaker: Dr Silvia Bertagnolio, WHO Unit Head for Surveillance, Evidence and Laboratory Strengthening, Division for AMR
a5866.speech: "When a patient requires antibiotics, the benefits often outweigh the risks associated with side effects or antibiotic resistance. However, when they are unnecessary, they offer no benefit while posing risks, and their use contributes to the emergence and spread of antimicrobial resistance."

a5866.speaker: Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa
a5866.speech: "AMR is not only a medical challenge, but rather a complex, multi-faceted burden that demands a whole-of-society response. Africa's health systems and economies cannot afford the cost of inaction, but with collaboration, it is possible to effectively mitigate the impact of AMR, and protect public health across the region."

a5866.speaker: Dr Casmir Ifeanyi, President of the Association of Medical Laboratory Scientists of Nigeria
a5866.speech: Said a study carried out a few years ago on an estuary in the country showed that high levels of antimicrobial agents were found in crabs and other crustaceans ; said this is an example of how huge the burden of AMR is and underscores the need for heightened public awareness and improved regulation of antimicrobials in all sectors ; called for the integration of training including for medical laboratory practitioners in the policies for AMR in the country ; added that patent medicine vendors should be stopped from stocking and vending antibiotics.

a5866.speaker: Ifeyinwa George, Pharmacist, DRASA Health Trust
a5866.speech: Said multisectoral involvement is key in ensuring sustainability and scalability of AMR mitigation and containment efforts ; "Lets get involved and drive the conversations that address AMR within our communities, states, country and continent. And as we think through viable AMR awareness campaign ideas, let's think One Health."

a5866.speaker: Dr Jide Idris, Director General of NCDC
a5866.speech: Said the organisation ensures that Nigeria's response is both strong and effective, working hand-in-hand with counterparts from human health, animal health, and environmental sectors under the One Health approach, raising antimicrobial resistance awareness, education, understanding, and behaviour change among all relevant stakeholders.

a5866.speaker: Prof Muhammad Ali Pate, Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare of Nigeria
a5866.speech: Said the launch of the National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) 2.0 came at a time when the global community, through platforms like the 2024 United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), had committed to renewed and urgent action against AMR.

a6103.speaker: Zain, MTN and Digitel (joint statement)
a6103.speech: Said the tariffs adjustment is made following an agreement with the National Communication Authority and the Bank of South Sudan, in response to recent increase in the official exchange rate: "This adjustment follows a thorough analysis of its potential impact on customers and the telecommunication sector. Henceforth, telecommunication service prices will be aligned with BoSS' official exchange rate." ; The statement said a similar change will follow on 18th November and 18th December.

a6103.speaker: Zain, MTN and Digitel (telecom operators)
a6103.speech: Emphasized "our commitment to providing customers with timely and transparent information regarding these changes." ; "We are dedicated to ensuring an exceptional experience for our customers, maintaining service quality, promoting inclusivity and driving digital transformation across the country through our ongoing network investments."

a6103.speaker: Juol Nhomngek, Member of Parliament
a6103.speech: Presented a motion concerning the reports that telecom networks are abnormally increasing the cost of their services, a situation he said had caused a major setback on the socio-economic welfare of the population.

a6103.speaker: The parliamentary motion (document)
a6103.speech: Explained that the high charges for internet and other communication services creates barriers to public awareness, making it difficult for people to access accurate and timely information.

a6210.speaker: Hakan Fidan, Turkish Minister of Foreign Affairs
a6210.speech: Reaffirmed Ankara’s support for Algiers’ position on the Sahel, stressing the importance of Algerian-Turkish cooperation in fighting terrorism and extremism: “Regarding the Sahel region, we consider that in order to resolve the problem of terrorism and extremism, we will continue to work together. We support the Algerian position, which perceives the resolution of regional issues with clarity and discernment.” ; Welcomed Algeria’s role on the UN Security Council, where it “successfully makes the concerns of our region heard.”

a6210.speaker: Hakan Fidan, Turkish Minister of Foreign Affairs
a6210.speech: On Gaza, insisted on the need to “intensify consultations” in order to deliver humanitarian aid and establish an immediate ceasefire.

a6210.speaker: Ahmed Attaf, Algerian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a6210.speech: Described the Algerian-Turkish partnership as “strategic”, highlighting the desire of the two countries to strengthen their cooperation: “The decision of our two Presidents to found this commission as an institutional space makes it possible to address common priorities and to remove the obstacles to their realisation.”

a6232.speaker: Joseph Nyuma Boakai, President of Liberia (special Message introducing the AAID dossier)
a6232.speech: "Liberia is a nation of untapped potential. Endowed with abundant natural resources, a strategic geographical location, and a youthful population - 74.6 percent of the population - is below 35 years old, Liberia possesses the building blocks for transformative growth. Yet, significant challenges persist. Governance challenges, the legacy of protracted conflict, global crises and persistent poverty has hindered progress. With many Liberians living in poverty and unemployment disproportionately affecting women and youth, we must take bold and innovative steps to achieve inclusive and sustainable development." ; "The AAID endeavors is to confront these challenges by prioritizing human capital development, economic transformation, and good governance as cornerstones of our development. We are committed to empowering Liberians by improving health and nutrition outcomes, providing quality education, and empowering our youth with technical and vocational training and skilling, thus creating employment opportunities for them, as they play a catalytic role in transforming Liberia."

a6232.speaker: Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, Finance and Development Planning Minister of Liberia (Foreword of the AAID document)
a6232.speech: "The AAID is underpinned by principles of inclusiveness, sustainability, justice and equality, accountability, peace and reconciliation, and local ownership. It reflects the aspirations of all Liberians, shaped by nationwide consultations with stakeholders including government, civil society, private sector actors, traditional leaders, the youth, People with Disabilities, and international partners. These consultations reinforced the importance of a people-centered development, addressing systemic barriers and structural inequalities while prioritizing the empowerment of marginalized communities."

a6255.speaker: International Human Rights Protection Service – Nigeria (IHRPS-N) (statement)
a6255.speech: Has expressed grief over the escalating bloodshed in Benue State, urging President Bola Tinubu to muster political will to end the massacre of Nigerian citizens.

a6255.speaker: Ambassador Blessing Joseph Afang, President, IHRPS-Nigeria
a6255.speech: Lamented the recent killings, stressing that between last week Friday night and the following day, in Yelewata alone, over 150 men, women, and children were brutally killed, homes and livelihoods destroyed in a single coordinated assault; stated these tragic events were not isolated, but form part of a broader and deepening humanitarian crisis in the country; stressed that survivors speak of charred bodies in markets and burnt crops, years of hard work reduced to ashes.

a6255.speaker: Amnesty International (investigation)
a6255.speech: Quoted by Afang as finding that over 6,800 lives had been lost in Benue since May 2023, and hundreds of villages razed.

a6255.speaker: Ambassador Blessing Joseph Afang, President, IHRPS-Nigeria
a6255.speech: “Our collective moral responsibility is undeniable. Under international human rights law and Nigeria's own Constitution, every person has the right to life, security, property, and dignity.” ; “These atrocities constitute grave violations of those rights. Impunity must end. Justice must begin.”

a6255.speaker: Ambassador Blessing Joseph Afang, President, IHRPS-Nigeria
a6255.speech: “IHRPS issues the following urgent demands: Swift and Impartial Investigations. The perpetrators must be hunted down, any affiliation with herdsmen, militias, or armed bandits investigated. No delay, no excuses.” ; “Security agencies must be held to account for any inaction that has allowed this bloodshed. Transparent Prosecution: Those responsible must face fair and public trials under federal jurisdiction. Their guilt or innocence must be determined in court—not in the absence of proper process.”

a6255.speaker: Ambassador Blessing Joseph Afang, President, IHRPS-Nigeria
a6255.speech: Calling for security architecture reform, noted that Nigeria's current security framework is fragmented and reactive: “The IHRC urges the Federal Government to commission comprehensive reforms focused on early-warning systems, community policing, and collaboration with local leaders.” ; “Technology must be harnessed, employing surveillance, geofencing, and conflict-resolution tools to preempt violence.”

a6255.speaker: Ambassador Blessing Joseph Afang, President, IHRPS-Nigeria
a6255.speech: Called for the protection of humanitarian rights and livelihoods: “With hundreds of thousands displaced and millions of livelihoods destroyed, immediate humanitarian assistance is non-negotiable.” ; “Extend emergency food, shelter, medical support, and forensics to identify victims. Moreover, replant farms and rebuild marketplaces to give people reasons to return home.”

a6255.speaker: Ambassador Blessing Joseph Afang, President, IHRPS-Nigeria
a6255.speech: Called for the bridging of farmers-herders divides, stressing that these recurring attacks were tied to underlying resource tensions – land, water, grazing rights – and that the solutions lie not in violence, but in structured dialogue: “We support calls from the Institute for Peace and Conflict Resolution for local-level roundtables, the gazetting of land, and cooperative pasture planning.”

a6255.speaker: Institute for Peace and Conflict Resolution
a6255.speech: Calls for local-level roundtables, the gazetting of land, and cooperative pasture planning.

a6255.speaker: Ambassador Blessing Joseph Afang, President, IHRPS-Nigeria
a6255.speech: “National Political Will and Accountability: This cannot be left to regional or local actors alone” ; “The Federal Government, led by Mr. President, must display decisive leadership.” ; “If state authorities fail, the central government must intervene, using constitutional powers when necessary – including, if warranted, emergency measures – against the plague of violence.”

a6255.speaker: Ambassador Blessing Joseph Afang, President, IHRPS-Nigeria
a6255.speech: Said that there cannot be neutrality in the face of genocide: “Silence betrays. Inaction denies justice to the dead and condemns the living. Our unity, dignity, and future depend on swift redress and reform.” ; “To the survivors in Makurdi and Yelewata, on behalf of the IHRPS, I extend heartfelt condolences. We mourn with you. We stand with you. And we will not relent until justice is served.” ; “To the government, we urge you to see this not merely as a regional conflict—but as a national emergency.” ; “The eyes of the world are upon Nigeria. We demand that the words spoken today be followed by deeds, transparency, and tangible change.” ; “Let this moment be the turning point. Let justice be our rallying cry. Let the Phoenix of Nigerian peace rise from these ashes.”

a6396.speaker: Ezra Chadzamira, Masvingo Minister of State for Provincial Affairs and Devolution
a6396.speech: Speaking at the commissioning of a US$1.1 million project in Rutenga, said the centre was in sync with the need to industrialise communities ; “The MSC aligns with the Government of Zimbabwe's Agriculture 8.0 drive that promotes Rural Industrialization as we move towards a knowledge-based, prosperous, and empowered upper-middle-income society by 2030, particularly around value addition and beneficiation, promotion of exports, employment creation, and youth development,” he said ; “The MSC also plays a crucial role in boosting the province's ambitious economic thrust towards achieving an eight-billion-dollar economy by 2030. SAT and its partners are commended for the sterling work they have undertaken in the last two years to put Mwenezi District and Masvingo Province on the map.”

a6396.speaker: Ezra Chadzamira, Masvingo Minister of State for Provincial Affairs and Devolution
a6396.speech: Said the growing of sesame and paprika augured well with the climate change being experienced, as drought-tolerant crops resilient in the face of low rainfall ; “The processing plants are important since they add value to the crops. Tichivaka dunhu redu reMasvingo, tichivaka nyika yedu ye Zimbabwe. I am reliably informed that the paprika processing mill has already produced and sold at least 20 tonnes of milled paprika for the local market, while 151 tonnes of sesame were exported to Itochu Corporation of Japan through Surface Wilmar in July 2024 and 61 tonnes of sesame were exported by SAT to Mozambique. The food safety certifications that are planned for later this year will unlock access to regional and global paprika markets, following product inquiries from South Africa, Spain, India, the United States of America, among others.” ; said the paprika mill can produce 300 tonnes of milled paprika a year which will guarantee access to a market on the doorsteps for smallholder farmers on irrigation schemes in the province.

a6431.speaker: Augustine Ngafuan, Liberia's Finance Minister
a6431.speech: In an appearance on the Voice of America (VOA), stated that canceling a $17 million USAID-sponsored project and other initiatives will directly and indirectly impact the country's development ; highlighted that USAID has been Liberia's second-largest donor, following the World Bank, supporting health, education, agriculture, and elections projects ; expressed confidence in Liberia's resilience and ability to overcome this latest obstacle in its development.

a6431.speaker: Malaria Indicator Survey of 2022
a6431.speech: According to the survey, the prevalence of malaria in children under five years old is 10%.

a6472.speaker: A resident (unnamed, Awka)
a6472.speech: “I have to trek back home from Eke Awka, nearly 3km because I have not seen Keke Napep from the market to Aroma Roundabout where I will take another Keke to my house. This is the most observed sit-at-home in the recent time.”

a6472.speaker: Kanayo Uzuegbu, Enugu State Commissioner of Police
a6472.speech: Issued a stern warning to pro-Biafra agitators, stating that any attempts to disrupt the state’s peace and security would be met with swift and decisive action.

a6472.speaker: Group claiming to be launching Biafran (pro-Biafra separatists)
a6472.speech: Had announced a two-day sit-at-home protest across five South Eastern states, as well as parts of Delta, Rivers, and Kogi states, scheduled for Monday, October 21, and Tuesday, October 22.

a6516.speaker: Gael Comhaire and Sonia Mrsic-Garac, two international experts who carried out studies on the cases of Benin and the DRC
a6516.speech: Observe that “Le manque d'organisation du réseau empêche les structures de coordination d'organiser des formations en vue du renforcement des capacités de la base. Le flux informationnel est déficitaire au sein du mouvement” (“The network's lack of organisation prevents the coordinating structures from organising training aimed at strengthening the capacities of the grassroots. The flow of information within the movement is deficient”) ; according to them, the effect of notability plays a strong role and the non-renewal of members is sharply criticised in both countries.

a6530.speaker: Abiy Ahmed, Prime Minister of Ethiopia
a6530.speech: Affirmed before parliament that Ethiopia is now recognized as Africa's leading wheat producer in both quantity and quality.

a6530.speaker: Farmers across various districts of Ethiopia
a6530.speech: Testify to the tangible benefits of summer irrigation, many now achieving multiple harvests annually compared to a single yield previously, with many reporting doubled outputs.

a6842.speaker: Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA)
a6842.speech: Granted the Gateway International Cargo Airport an Interim Aerodrome Operational Permit on Friday, August 15, 2025, allowing the airport to operate scheduled commercial air transport flights; described the airport as a model for future aviation infrastructure in Nigeria.

a6842.speaker: Combined team of regulatory authorities including the NCAA, Nigerian Airspace Management Agency (NAMA) and Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet)
a6842.speech: Hailed the quality of facilities put in place as one of the best in West Africa, unanimously concluding that the infrastructure at the airport, including the Control Tower, Weather Monitoring Areas, Runway, Fire Service Stations, and the Apron, could rival any of their type around the world.

a6842.speaker: Dapo Abiodun, Governor of Ogun State
a6842.speech: Has been explicit that the state government’s investment was to de-risk the project and attract private capital.

a6842.speaker: Ogun State government
a6842.speech: Has made it clear that the airport will be run on a concession basis.

a7059.speaker: Nikki Haley, US Ambassador to the United Nations
a7059.speech: Warned the international community, which is to vote next Thursday on a resolution condemning Washington’s recent recognition of Jerusalem as the capital of Israel; assured that the United States will not hesitate to take down the names of the countries that go against this resolution.

a7059.speaker: United States government (Twitter post)
a7059.speech: Washington also used Twitter to send a clear message: “On Thursday there will be a vote criticising our choice. The United States will be taking names.”

a7107.speaker: UNOCHA (data cited)
a7107.speech: According to the UNOCHA, at least five million Nigerians in the BAY States (Borno, Adamawa and Yobe) got humanitarian assistance from the United Nations organs in each of the last 10 years.

a7107.speaker: Trond Jensen, Head of OCHA Nigeria
a7107.speech: Disclosed this at a press conference to mark the UN's 78th anniversary, however, said more needed to be done to resolve the crisis in the North East ; said stakeholders must go beyond humanitarian assistance and invest more in the development of the North East to resolve the humanitarian crisis in the region ; while noting that the humanitarian situation in the BAY states was getting worse, said 300 million were currently in need of humanitarian assistance compared to 81 million in 2014.

a7107.speaker: Elsie Attafuah, UNDP Resident Representative in Nigeria
a7107.speech: Said the organisation was taking a different approach in addressing the issues in the North West ; also said the UN is collaborating with universities in Nigeria to support innovation among the youths in the country.

a7107.speaker: Mohamed Fall, Resident Coordinator of the UN in Nigeria
a7107.speech: Said the organisation's activities cut across the country, adding that more interest was being given to the North West as a result of banditry and farmers/herders crisis: "I think our engagement is also based on what we have done in the North East and I just want to remind you of a few principles. The first one is that we are not going to engage in the North West by dropping the North East because we see increasing demand. In the North East, we are engaging development solution, and we are engaging into medium and longer-term development. In the North West, the operation will be led by the government. It will not be something that the UN will lead but UN will be behind the government."

a7107.speaker: Mohamed Fall, Resident Coordinator of the UN in Nigeria
a7107.speech: Added that the UN is currently looking at localisation of humanitarian assistance because of dwindling funding: "We have extensively used international partners, but now there is a conversation growing in the humanitarian world and in the developing world, which is around localisation, because that's the way you make sure that when the operation finishes, you leave something there, and you leave capacity there. Localisation, because it's more efficient and less costly in terms of business model, is the way that you make sure that you are coming in assistance, that it's people to really have to own their own response, to have their own development process."

a7171.speaker: Dr. Sam Onyia, USAID State2State Team Lead
a7171.speech: In his welcome remarks, explained that Open Government Partnership (OGP) is a global initiative that brings together governments, civil society organizations and citizens to promote transparency, accountability, and citizen engagement in governance ; Stated that it was launched in the year 2011, and was to protect civil space and provide civil liberty in Nigeria both at National and Sub National levels ; He said the workshop reviewed and updated the cost implementation plan of SAP2 in Ebonyi State so as to align it with the proposal for SAP3 ; He added that it would also conduct on boarding for the newly constituted steering committee to understand their roles and responsibilities, and synergize their activities with the OGP technical working groups in driving OGP implementation.

a7171.speaker: Chief Mathias Adum, Principal Secretary to the Ebonyi State Governor and Co-Chairman of OGP (Government side)
a7171.speech: In an opening remarks, thanked the USAID State2State for their various interventions, activities, trainings and programmes aimed at ensuring good governance in Ebonyi State ; He solicited for the inclusion of the local government in the OGP thematic working groups so as to integrate the grassroots ; He assured of the supports and cooperation of Ebonyi State Government in the effective and successful implementation of the State Action Plan3.

a7171.speaker: Mr. Oliver Aja Chima, OGP Co-Chair in charge of the civil society
a7171.speech: Urged the participants to place much emphasis on collaboration between government and civil society organizations for continued fruitful engagement, adding that the review meeting will help to improve on the implementation of the SAP3.

a7171.speaker: Ejiro Okotie, Gender and Social Inclusion Specialist and OGP focal person for State2State
a7171.speech: In a presentation on mainstreaming GESI in OGP State Action Plan, said it would provide the participants with the tools and GESI principles to make the implementation of the State Action Plan more inclusive.

a7171.speaker: Mr Uchenna Arisukwu, national secretariat of OGP
a7171.speech: Delivered lectures on understanding the Open Government Partnership (OGP) Process and Commitment, maintaining that the OGP is a policy approach to governance reforms that aimed to build a culture of transparency, civic participation and accountability that increase confidence in government and equally strengthen social contacts.

a7171.speaker: Mr. Mooreino Diftuffe, Monitoring and Evaluation Specialist, OGP National Secretariat
a7171.speech: Presented modalities for Delivery of State Action Plan3 and highlighted the basic needs for the programme team on how to carry out their roles and responsibilities towards managing for results.

a7171.speaker: Chief Romanus Nwasum, Chairman of Ebonyi State Local Government Service Commission, and Mrs. Blessing Uche Edene, Clerk of the State House of Assembly
a7171.speech: In a vote of thanks at the end of the workshop, commended the USAID State2State for their partnership with Ebonyi State which they said had helped in reshaping the future of the state and the people. They assured of the continuity of the programme in Ebonyi State.

a7263.speaker: Benoit Daviron and Stefano Ponte, authors of “The Coffee Paradox: Global Markets, Commodity Trade & The Elusive Promise of Development”
a7263.speech: Revealed how a thriving coffee market in consuming countries contrasts with mounting crises in producing regions, and attribute the widening gap between the raw coffee bean price and the final product cost mainly to oligopolistic rent captured by Western-based coffee roasting giants.

a7263.speaker: Overseas Development Institute (ODI), a London-based think-tank (study)
a7263.speech: A study exposed this disparity: it found that if Ethiopia's coffee exports to the EU were halted under the EUDR, the country could lose its largest market; with 30pc of Ethiopian coffee bound for Europe, such a blow could spur an economic downturn, exacerbate poverty, and deepen inequality.

a7263.speaker: Original Food GmbH, German coffee buyer
a7263.speech: Allegedly claimed to be the exclusive buyer of coffee from Ethiopia's Kaffa and Bonga areas, patented local names such as “Bonga Red Mountain” and “KaffaLand”, then sued other foreign and Ethiopian buyers of Kaffa coffee, asserting it held a legal permit in Ethiopia to monopolise sales in Europe.

a7263.speaker: Ethiopian Coffee & Tea Authority (ECTA) (statement of January 24, 2025)
a7263.speech: Addressed the dispute in a statement, saying that, working with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Intellectual Property Protection Agency, the Federal Cooperatives Commission, and others, the Authority monitored the legal proceedings to counter Original Food's monopolistic tactics and improper market behavior, and that after conducting the necessary assessment and providing evidence on the matter it banned the company from buying coffee in Ethiopia.

a7263.speaker: Owner of Original Food GmbH
a7263.speech: Apologized publicly, vowing to adopt more equitable marketing strategies.

a7274.speaker: Umodzi Party (statement signed by Party President Hon. Thomas Wezzie Kaumba)
a7274.speech: Praised the government's decision to pause the Extended Credit Facility (ECF) arrangement with the International Monetary Fund, describing it as a "bold and positive" step toward economic independence ; "For decades, Malawi's economy has relied heavily on foreign aid and loans. This decision marks a turning point towards building a truly self-reliant economy," noting that the country's public debt, now over K12 trillion, has placed immense pressure on citizens.

a7274.speaker: Umodzi Party (statement signed by Party President Hon. Thomas Wezzie Kaumba)
a7274.speech: Strongly condemned recent incidents of political violence in the lead-up to the elections, urging the Malawi Police Service to investigate and prosecute all perpetrators: "Political violence has no place in modern Malawi. We call on all 23 registered political parties to sign a peace accord to demonstrate their commitment to unity."

a7274.speaker: Umodzi Party (statement signed by Party President Hon. Thomas Wezzie Kaumba)
a7274.speech: Threw its full support behind the use of Smartmatic electronic voting technology, emphasizing that digital innovation is vital for enhancing transparency and aligning Malawi's electoral process with global democratic standards, and criticizing opposition parties that have raised concerns: "We are not surprised that those who manipulated the 2019 elections with duplicate votes and correction fluid are now opposing Smartmatic. This technology ensures a credible vote, and we urge the Malawi Electoral Commission to remain resolute."

a7274.speaker: Umodzi Party (statement signed by Party President Hon. Thomas Wezzie Kaumba)
a7274.speech: Confirmed it will not field a presidential candidate in the 2025 elections and will instead support President Chakwera and the Malawi Congress Party, citing ongoing development under the current administration; highlighted improvements in infrastructure, social support programmes, increased student loan access and electricity reliability as key achievements since the Tonse Alliance took office: "This government is delivering development without discrimination. Supporting President Chakwera is the only logical choice for those who love Malawi." ; described President Chakwera as "the Joshua" who will lead the nation to prosperity, and said "Let us not take five steps backwards. The Canaan we seek is within reach. Malawi needs unity. Malawi needs Umodzi."

a7274.speaker: Umodzi Party (statement signed by Party President Hon. Thomas Wezzie Kaumba)
a7274.speech: Dismissed speculation about a possible alliance with the UTM, describing the party as "an amateur" lacking national focus.

a7351.speaker: Rodinald Soomer, CEO of the CARICOM Development Fund (CDF)
a7351.speech: underlined the importance of the partnership for advancing the Caribbean’s sustainable development agenda: “This grant from Afreximbank will enable the CDF to strengthen its support to CARICOM member states that have to confront the urgent environmental and economic challenges of our time. The Green Resilience and Sustainability Facility is an essential step towards ensuring long-term resilience and economic sustainability.”

a7351.speaker: Professor Oramah, President of Afreximbank and of the Bank’s Board of Directors
a7351.speech: remarked: “The GRSF will provide a means of catalysing and mobilising investment to support Caribbean countries facing economic and fiscal challenges arising from the impact of frequent and intense adverse weather events associated with climate change. It will also serve as a mechanism for financing climate-related loss and damage and for building resilience, which will mitigate the impacts and give the member states of the Caribbean Community the means to confront these challenges, with a view to closing the region’s US$20 billion resilience financing gap.”

a7351.speaker: CARICOM Development Fund (CDF)
a7351.speech: recognises that the region’s development challenges are becoming increasingly complex, and that most of these problems can be solved through market-based solutions.

a7380.speaker: Coalition for Democratic Change (CDC) (official response to the State of the Nation Address)
a7380.speech: Said it is delivering a speech in response to the State of the Nation Address for the first time in its history, choosing to speak directly to the Liberian people "because of the grave instability and uncertainty that now hang over our democracy and economy. Our nation is in crisis. The state of the nation is weak, divided and polarized," evident when about eight Senators, more than 25 representatives, and the entire Supreme Court bench boycotted President Boakai's SONA. ; "Liberia is in decline. The democratic and economic gains we made in the last six years are being eroded. We now see the Unity Party trapped in the very lies they sold the Liberian people to get elected."

a7380.speaker: Coalition for Democratic Change (CDC) (official response to the State of the Nation Address)
a7380.speech: Said that one year after the peaceful transfer of power, "Liberia now lies in a democratic and rule of law mess," and that the Unity Party administration "is now teaching the Liberian people that the rule of law has no meaning or no value"; said citizens are beaten and wounded for exercising constitutional rights, opposition personalities and former officials are being witch-hunted and unjustly imprisoned, and that the Executive has imposed an illegally selected Speaker upon Liberia while seeking the resignation of the duly elected Speaker - "What a mockery of democracy and the rule of law!"

a7380.speaker: Coalition for Democratic Change (CDC) (official response to the State of the Nation Address)
a7380.speech: Said the Unity Party "packaged a massive bundle of lies and sold those lies to the Liberian people" - on harmonization, drugs, roads, private jets, commodity prices and the exchange rate - and that one year later the reality has set in; said the price of basic commodities has increased and the UP Government has admitted in the illegally passed 2025 National Budget that the exchange rate may reach as high as LRD 219 to US$1.00 in 2025, showing that the "country is hard," that the "Rescue Mission has now become the Excuse Mission," and that Liberians should prepare for the worst economic situation in 2025.

a7380.speaker: Coalition for Democratic Change (CDC) (official response to the State of the Nation Address)
a7380.speech: Said President Boakai's speech "was packed with misinformation in so many areas," and moved to correct it: that the reported US$734 million revenue against US$661.4 million spent implies a US$72.6 million surplus absent from the 2025 budget, so either it "was blown off in massive act of corruption or everything the president said about 2024 revenue was false and misleading"; that the price of rice rose from LR$3,100 to LR$3,500 for a 25kg bag; that harmonization is still the prevailing policy; that instead of removing 6,000 workers the UP hired about 6,000, increasing the payroll by about US$10 million; and that the international climate financing cited - the US$25 million Monrovia Metropolitan Climate Resilience Project financed by the Green Climate Fund - was secured by the CDC administration.

a7380.speaker: Coalition for Democratic Change (CDC) (official response to the State of the Nation Address)
